In the unweighted setting, complexities are computed using the best known bound on the matrix multiplication exponent $\omega\leq 2.371339$ from [ADV+25]. The stated bound for [Mao22] additionally uses results on Rectangular Bounded Monotone Min-plus Product by Dürr [Dür23].*

A third question concerns the unweighted TED problem. Mao [Mao22] showed that a truly subcubic running time is possible for the problem. The current record for the running time is by Dürr [Dür23] and is $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{(4\omega+12)/(\omega+5})=\mathcal{O}(n^{2.9148})$ .11 1 $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}$ hides poly-logarithmic factors. Here, $\omega$ is the $n\times n$ matrix multiplication exponent, where one can multiply two $n\times n$ matrices in $\mathcal{O}(n^{\omega+\varepsilon})$ time for all $\varepsilon>0$ .22 2 Slightly abusing notation, we omit this $\varepsilon$ from the rest of the paper, which is in line with the literature. The reader should be aware that in many running times in the literature that one states in terms of $\omega$ , a secret $\varepsilon$ is always hiding. The running times with a numerical-valued exponent use a strict upper bound on $\omega$ (such as the $\mathcal{O}(n^{2.9546})$ running time for unweighted TED of [Mao22]), so this $\varepsilon$ does not appear. The current bound on $\omega$ , due to [ADV+25], is $\omega\leq 2.371339$ .

There are many structured variants of problems related to APSP and for a very large number of them, shortly after a truly subcubic time algorithm was found, an $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{(3+\omega)/2})$ time (or better) algorithm was also found. There are many such examples, we present a few:

- • The All Pairs Bottleneck Paths [VWY09] and All pairs nondecreasing paths [Vas10] problems were first shown to have truly subcubic time algorithms in the first decade of the century and are now both known to be solvable in $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{(3+\omega)/2})$ time [DJW19, DP09].

- • The Min-Plus product of $n\times n$ matrices (given $A,B$ , compute $C$ with $C[i,j]=\min_{k}(A[i,k]+B[k,j]$ ) is known to be equivalent to APSP in $n$ -node graphs [FM71] so that under the APSP Hypothesis it requires $n^{3-o(1)}$ time. Various structured variants of the Min-Plus matrix product have been shown to have truly subcubic time algorithms, e.g. when the matrices have “bounded differences” [BGSV19] or whose entries are bounded by $\mathcal{O}(n)$ and are monotone (non-decreasing in the rows or columns) [VX20, GPVX21]. Later, [CDXZ22] showed that these variants can be solved in $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{(3+\omega)/2})$ time. These structured Min-Plus products have many applications for a variety of fundamental problems, e.g. to many sequence similarity problems such as Language Edit Distance (aka Scored Parsing [AP72, Sah17, BGHS19]), RNA Folding [NJ80, Aku99, ZTZU11, VGF14, Sah17] and Dyck Edit Distance [Sah14, BGHS19, DKS22, FGK+24]. All of these problems now have $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{(3+\omega)/2})$ time algorithms.

As TED seems related to APSP and since its unweighted version is now known to have a truly subcubic algorithm, a natural question is:

Question 3: Can unweighted TED be solved in $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{(3+\omega)/2})$ time?

Mao’s truly subcubic time algorithm for unweighted TED [Mao22] can be viewed as a reduction to Bounded Monotone Min-Plus product which can be solved in $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{(3+\omega)/2})$ time. The reduction, however, is not efficient enough to achieve the same running time for unweighted TED. One way to resolve Question 3 is by presenting a tight reduction. Is such a reduction possible?

#### Our Results.

We resolve all three questions above. Similarly to the prior work on TED, we focus on solving the more general edit distance problem on ordered forests (rather than just single trees): collections of rooted trees with a left-to-right ordering. Our first main theorem is a fine-grained reduction from (forest) TED to the Min-Plus product problem mentioned earlier:

Min-Plus Matrix Multiplication (MUL) Input: Two $m\times m$ matrices $A=(a_{i,j})$ and $B=(b_{i,j})$ . Output: The distance matrix $C=A\star B$ , where $C=(c_{i,j})$ is defined as $c_{i,j}=\min_{k\in\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,m\,\bm{]}}\{a_{i,k}+b_{k,j}\}$ .

Let $\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(N)$ denote the running time for solving MUL on two $N\times N$ matrices, or equivalently ([FM71]) for solving APSP in $N$ node graphs.

The formal theorem for our reduction is as follows: {mtheorem}[] Let $\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ be forests of size $n=\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert,m=\left\lvert\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\right\rvert$ with $n\geq m$ . Then, there is an algorithm computing Tree Edit Distance between $\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ in time $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left((n/m)^{1+o(1)}\cdot\left(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(m)+m^{2+o(1)}\right)\right)$ .

If $m=n$ , the theorem states that TED on $n$ -node forests can be solved in $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(n))$ . We thus complete the missing direction in establishing the equivalence between TED and APSP, resolving Question 2.

In fact, because our reduction is very efficient and only adds polylogarithmic factors over the APSP running time, we are also able to resolve Question 1 using Williams’ [Wil18] $m^{3}/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log m})}$ running time for APSP.

#### Corollary 1.1.

Let $\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ be forests. Then, there is an algorithm for TED running in time $n^{3}/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}$ , where $n=\max(|\mathbf{F}|,|\mathbf{F}^{\prime}|)$ . \lipicsEnd

Beyond providing a faster algorithm for TED, Corollary 1.1 underscores once again the difference in nature between ED and TED by demonstrating that, while we (probably) cannot eliminate an arbitrary number of logarithmic factors for the former, we can do so for the latter.

The last several TED algorithms (prior to ours) all use the same dynamic programming approach which was formalized as a decomposition framework for solving TED [DT03, DT05]. Formalizing the framework allowed for proving lower bounds on the running time of any algorithm that falls into that framework. The first such lower bound was by [DT03] who showed such algorithms must take $\Omega(n^{2}\log^{2}n)$ time. The approach culminated in obtaining an $\Omega(n^{3})$ time lower bound [DMRW10] for any algorithm that falls within the framework. Since our algorithm runs faster than cubic time, it falls outside the framework.

We also resolve Question 3 by providing an $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{(3+\omega)/2})$ time algorithm for unweighted TED. This is a significant improvement over Mao’s result [Mao22].

We achieve our result via a tight reduction to the Bounded Monotone Min-Plus product problem.

Bounded Monotone Min-Plus Matrix Multiplication (MonMUL) Input: An $m\times n$ matrix $A=(a_{i,j})$ and an $n\times\ell$ matrix $B=(b_{i,j})$ such that either for all $i\in[m],j\in[n]$ , $a_{i,j}\leq a_{i,j+1}$ (“row-monotone”) or for all $i\in[m],j\in[n]$ , $a_{i,j}\leq a_{i+1,j}$ (“column-monotone”). Output: The distance matrix $C=A\star B$ , where $C=(c_{i,j})$ is defined as $c_{i,j}=\min_{k\in\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,n\,\bm{]}}\{a_{i,k}+b_{k,j}\}$ .

When $m=n=\ell$ and $D=\mathcal{O}(n)$ , MonMUL can be solved in $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{(3+\omega)/2})$ [CDXZ22].

We denote by $\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(m,n,\ell,D)$ the running time for computing MonMUL. When $m=n=\ell=D$ , we simply write $\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(m)$ for the running time of MonMUL.

[] Let $\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ be two forests of size $n=\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert,m=\left\lvert\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\right\rvert$ with $n\geq m$ . Suppose that $\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(N,N,N,\mathrm{D})=\mathcal{O}(f(N)g(\mathrm{D}))$ . Then, there is an algorithm computing Unweighted Tree Edit Distance between $\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ in time $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left((n/m)^{1+o(1)}\cdot\left(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(m)+m^{2+o(1)}g(m)\right)\right)$ .

The best known bound for the MonMUL running time [CDXZ22, Dür23] is $\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(N,N,N,D)=\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(N^{(2+\omega)/2}D^{1/2})$ . Hence, Section 1 implies that given two forests of equal size, we can compute Unweighted Tree Edit Distance in $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(m^{(3+\omega)/2})$ time, matching the complexity of bounded monotone min-plus product [CDXZ22] and resolving Question 3.

More generally, we obtain the following result.

#### Corollary 1.2.

There is an algorithm for Unweighted TED running in time $n^{1+o(1)}m^{(1+\omega)/2}$ , where $n=\max(|\mathbf{F}|,|\mathbf{F}^{\prime}|),m=\min(|\mathbf{F}|,|\mathbf{F}^{\prime}|)$ . \lipicsEnd

#### At the core of our results: TED alignment graphs.

The edit distance between two length- $n$ strings can be represented by examining the classical dynamic computation on an $\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,(n+1)\,\bm{]}\times\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,(n+1)\,\bm{]}$ grid. The solution is then traced by following the shortest path from $(1,1)$ to $(n+1,n+1)$ . Such graph-based representation is commonly referred to as an alignment graph.

The power of this representation is evident in the numerous results for string ED that have either emerged directly from this visualization or can be clearly illustrated through it (including but not limited to [LV88, Tis06, CKW23, GKS19, CKW23, KNW24, GJKT24, CKM20, DGH+23, GK24]). Consequently, it is not surprising that specific properties of alignment graphs, such as border-to-border distances, play a central role. For string ED, these distances can be computed in $\mathcal{O}(n^{2})$ time [Sch95, Tis06, ACS08, Kle05].

Alignment graphs for TED were introduced as a counterpart to those for ED and serve as a visualization tool for TED solutions. However, they appear predominantly in less recent works [Tou05, BCH+07, MTWZU09] and have played a less central role than in ED.

In this work, we reestablish the alignment graph for TED as a central tool and demonstrate that it provides a more powerful language and visualization framework for capturing the combinatorial structure of solutions than previously recognized. As a technical contribution, we show that in the alignment graph for TED, border-to-border distances can be computed in APSP time, while for unweighted TED, they can be determined in $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{(3+\omega)/2})$ .

#### Prior attempts to reduce TED to APSP and MUL.

At least two prior papers have attempted to leverage min-plus products for computing TED. The first of these works was by Chen [Che01], who introduced a dynamic programming scheme formulated using applications of MUL. However, this did not result in a true reduction, as the algorithm ran in $\mathcal{O}(n^{4})$ time (Chen initially claimed a running time of $\mathcal{O}(n^{3.5})$ , but this was later corrected in [SPA17]). The second work, by [Mao22], uses bounded difference min-plus products (a special case of bounded monotone min-plus multiplication) to achieve truly subcubic time for the unweighted (and very small weight) tree edit distance problem. However, Mao’s scheme was not powerful enough to achieve a fine-grained reduction from the general weight case of TED to MUL.

#### Other related works.

Recently, there has been significant interest in TED approximation algorithms [BGHS19, SS22] as well as TED when the distance is bounded [AJ21, DGH+22, DGH+23].

## 2 Techical Overview

### 2.1 Similarity and alignment graphs

We examine TED through its mapping formulation (as in [Mao22]). This means that rather than thinking of TED as finding a least-cost transformation via insertions, deletions, and matches, we shift our perspective towards seeking a maximum weight mapping between two forests.

#### String similarity.

To ease into this formulation, we first discuss the mapping formulation of (weighted) string edit distance. In the (String) Edit Distance Problem (ED), we are given two strings $A=a_{1}a_{2}\cdots a_{n}$ and $B=b_{1}b_{2}\cdots b_{m}$ , and a cost function $\delta$ . The goal is to find the least cost needed to transform $A$ into $B$ , by substituting, inserting or deleting characters. The costs $\delta(a_{i},b_{j})$ , $\delta(a_{i},\varepsilon)$ , and $\delta(\varepsilon,b_{j})$ describe the cost of substituting $a_{i}$ with $b_{j}$ , deleting $a_{i}$ , and inserting $b_{j}$ , respectively.

We define $\eta(a_{i},b_{j})\coloneqq\delta(a_{i},\varepsilon)+\delta(\varepsilon,b_{j})-\delta(a_{i},b_{j})$ to be the weight of matching $a_{i}$ with $b_{j}$ . Determining the string edit distance between $A$ and $B$ translates into calculating the similarity between $A$ and $B$ , defined as

$$ \mathsf{sim}(A,B)=\max\nolimits_{\begin{subarray}{c}i_{1}<\cdots<i_{k}\in\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,n\,\bm{]}\\
j_{1}<\cdots<j_{k}\in\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,m\,\bm{]}\end{subarray}}\Big\{\ \eta(a_{i_{1}},b_{j_{1}})+\eta(a_{i_{2}},b_{j_{2}})+\cdots+\eta(a_{i_{k}},b_{j_{k}})\ \Big\}. $$

Thereby, we obtain $\mathsf{sim}(A,B)=\sum_{i}\delta(a_{i},\varepsilon)+\sum_{j}\delta(\varepsilon,b_{j})-\mathsf{ed}(A,B)$ .

#### String alignment graphs.

The value $\mathsf{sim}(A,B)$ can be computed using the following recurrence

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{sim}(A,B)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{@{\;}c@{\quad}l@{}}0,&\text{if $|A|=0$ or $|B|=0$,}\\
\max\left\{\begin{aligned} &\mathsf{sim}(A\bm{[}\,2\,\bm{.\,.}\,n\,\bm{]},B),\\
&\mathsf{sim}(A,B\bm{[}\,2\,\bm{.\,.}\,m\,\bm{]}),\\
&\mathsf{sim}(A\bm{[}\,2\,\bm{.\,.}\,n\,\bm{]},B\bm{[}\,2\,\bm{.\,.}\,m\,\bm{]})+\eta(a_{1},b_{1})\end{aligned}\right\},&\text{otherwise}.\end{array}\right. $$

These computations can be reformulated as finding a longest path on a directed weighted acyclic graph, commonly referred to as the alignment graph. This graph has as the vertex set the grid $\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,(n+1)\,\bm{]}\times\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,(m+1)\,\bm{]}$ , where each node $(i,j)$ is connected with an edge of weight zero to its right and upper neighbors, i.e., $(i+1,j)$ and $(i,j+1)$ , if they are within the borders. Additionally, from each node $(i,j)\in\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,n\,\bm{]}\times\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,m\,\bm{]}$ , there is an edge to $(i+1,j+1)$ with weight $\eta(a_{i},b_{j})$ . Computing $\mathsf{sim}(A,B)$ translates to finding a longest path between $(1,1)$ and $(n+1,m+1)$ in this graph. Each time the longest path traverses an edge from $(i,j)$ to $(i+1,j+1)$ we map $a_{i}$ to $b_{j}$ .

It is worth noting that in the literature several studies [Sch95, Tis06, ACS08, Kle05] have focused on computing all longest distances from the lower-left border to the upper-right border in an alignment graph. For both weighted and unweighted edit distance, this task can be accomplished in time $\mathcal{O}((n+m)^{2})$ .

#### Tree similarity.

Similarly, given two forests $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ , define $\eta(v,v^{\prime})\coloneqq\delta(v,\varepsilon)+\delta(\varepsilon,v^{\prime})-\delta(v,v^{\prime})$ . The mapping we consider for TED corresponds to two sequences of distinct nodes $v_{1},\ldots v_{k}\in\mathbf{F}$ and $v_{1}^{\prime},\ldots v_{k}^{\prime}\in\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ such that for all $1\leq i<j\leq k$ :

- • $v_{i}$ is an ancestor of $v_{j}$ in $\mathbf{F}$ if and only if $v_{i}^{\prime}$ is an ancestor of $v_{j}^{\prime}$ in $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ ,

- • $v_{j}$ is an ancestor of $v_{i}$ in $\mathbf{F}$ if and only if $v_{j}^{\prime}$ is an ancestor of $v_{i}^{\prime}$ in $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ , and

- • if neither $v_{i}$ nor $v_{j}$ is the ancestor of the other, $v_{i}$ comes before $v_{j}$ in the pre-order traversal of $\mathbf{F}$ if and only if $v_{i}^{\prime}$ comes before $v_{j}^{\prime}$ in the pre-order traversal of $\mathbf{F}$ .

The similarity between $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ , denoted as $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime})$ , maximizes $\sum_{1\leq i\leq k}{\eta(v_{i},v_{i}^{\prime})}$ , where the maximum is taken over all such mappings.

As for strings, $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime})=\sum_{v\in\mathbf{F}}\delta(v,\varepsilon)+\sum_{v^{\prime}\in\mathbf{F}^{\prime}}\delta(\varepsilon,v^{\prime})-\mathsf{ed}(\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime})$ .

#### Forest alignment graphs.

Suppose we are given $\mathsf{sim}(\mathsf{sub}(v),\mathsf{sub}(v^{\prime}))$ for all $v\in\mathbf{F}$ and $v^{\prime}\in\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ , where $\mathsf{sub}(v)$ indicates the subtree rooted at node $v$ . Then, the value $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime})$ can be computed using Shasha and Zhang’s recurrence scheme [SZ89]. Given forests $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ with pre-order $v_{1},\ldots,v_{|\mathbf{F}|}$ and $v_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,v_{|\mathbf{F}^{\prime}|}^{\prime}$ , they compute:

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime})=\left\{\begin{array}[]{@{\;}c@{\quad}l@{}}0,&\text{if $\mathbf{F}=\varnothing$ or $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}=\varnothing$,}\\
\max\left\{\begin{aligned} &\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\setminus v_{1},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}),\\
&\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\setminus v_{1}^{\prime}),\\
&\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\setminus\mathsf{sub}(v_{1}),\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\setminus\mathsf{sub}(v_{1}^{\prime}))+\mathsf{sim}(\mathsf{sub}(v_{1}),\mathsf{sub}(v_{1}^{\prime}))\end{aligned}\right\},&\text{otherwise}.\end{array}\right. $$

Once again, these computations can be rephrased as finding the longest path in a directed acyclic graph with a grid as the vertex set, but only under the condition that we have the values $\mathsf{sim}(\mathsf{sub}(v),\mathsf{sub}(v^{\prime}))$ for all $v\in\mathbf{F}$ and $v^{\prime}\in\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ . With this condition in place, we can construct a grid $\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,(\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert+1)\,\bm{]}\times\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,(\left\lvert\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\right\rvert+1)\,\bm{]}$ . Similar to the case of strings, each node $(i,i^{\prime})$ is connected to its right and upper neighbors with an edge of weight zero, i.e., $(i+1,i^{\prime})$ and $(i,i^{\prime}+1)$ (if they are within the borders). Additionally, from each node $(i,i^{\prime})\in\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert\,\bm{]}\times\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,\left\lvert\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\right\rvert\,\bm{]}$ , there is an edge to $(j,j^{\prime})$ with weight $\mathsf{sim}(\mathsf{sub}(v_{i}),\mathsf{sub}(v_{i^{\prime}}^{\prime}))$ . Here, $j$ and $j^{\prime}$ are the smallest integers $j\geq i$ and $j^{\prime}\geq i^{\prime}$ such that $v_{j}\notin\mathsf{sub}(v_{i})$ and $v_{j^{\prime}}^{\prime}\notin\mathsf{sub}(v_{i^{\prime}}^{\prime})$ .

For an illustration (and a more formal definition) of such an alignment graph, refer to Figure 6 in Section 4, where we reduce to APSP the problem of computing all longest distances from the lower-left border to the upper-right in a forest alignment graph.

### 2.2 Warm-up: TED on caterpillar trees.

To better understand our algorithm for TED, let us first examine a more restricted yet significant case.

#### Caterpillar trees.

Caterpillar trees consist of a central path with nodes labeled $c_{1},c_{2},\ldots,c_{n}$ , where $c_{1}$ is the root. Additional, each central node $c_{i}$ has both a left child $l_{i}$ and a right child $r_{i}$ .33 3 In standard literature, caterpillar trees can take a more general form. Here, we focus on a specific type of caterpillar tree, though we continue to refer to them simply as caterpillar trees.

*Figure 1: Overlaying the alignment graphs for string edit distance for $(L,L^{\prime})$ and $(R,R^{\prime})$ leads to an intuitive visualization of TED on caterpillar trees under the assumption that central nodes are only mapped to central nodes, left children only to left ones, and right children only to right ones (Assumption A). The problem can be visualized as two paths in the two graphs, which, whenever they intersect, allow mapping of central nodes to central nodes.*

Let us examine the similarity mapping for two such caterpillar trees $\mathbf{T}$ and $\mathbf{T}^{\prime}$ , of size $\left\lvert\mathbf{T}\right\rvert=3n,\left\lvert\mathbf{T}^{\prime}\right\rvert=3n^{\prime}$ with node sets $\{l_{i},c_{i},r_{i}\}_{i\in\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,n\,\bm{]}}$ and $\{l_{i}^{\prime},c_{i}^{\prime},r_{i}^{\prime}\}_{i\in\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,n^{\prime}\,\bm{]}}$ . We examine such a mapping under an additional simplifying assumption: nodes from one side of the caterpillar $\mathbf{T}$ are always mapped to nodes of the same side of the caterpillar $\mathbf{T}^{\prime}$ .

#### Assumption A.

The nodes $\{c_{i}\}_{i}$ , $\{l_{i}\}_{i}$ and $\{r_{i}\}_{i}$ are always only mapped by $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{T},\mathbf{T}^{\prime})$ to nodes in $\{c_{i}^{\prime}\}_{i}$ , $\{l_{i}^{\prime}\}_{i}$ and $\{r_{i}^{\prime}\}_{i}$ , respectively. \lipicsEnd

Under Assumption A, suppose $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{T},\mathbf{T}^{\prime})$ maps $c_{i}$ to $c_{i^{\prime}}^{\prime}$ and $c_{j}$ to $c_{j^{\prime}}^{\prime}$ for $i<j$ , and no further node $c_{i+1},\ldots,c_{j-1}$ is mapped. Then, the nodes from $l_{i},\ldots,l_{j-1}$ are mapped to nodes from $l_{i^{\prime}}^{\prime},\ldots,l_{j^{\prime}-1^{\prime}}$ as in $\mathsf{sim}(L\bm{[}\,i\,\bm{.\,.}\,j\,\bm{)},L^{\prime}\bm{[}\,i^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,j^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ , where $L=l_{1}\cdots l_{n},L^{\prime}=l_{1^{\prime}}^{\prime}\cdots l_{n^{\prime}}^{\prime}$ are strings built from the left children of the central nodes. Similarly, the nodes from $r_{i},\ldots,r_{j-1}$ are mapped to nodes from $r_{i^{\prime}}^{\prime},\ldots,r_{j^{\prime}-1^{\prime}}$ as in $\mathsf{sim}(R\bm{[}\,i\,\bm{.\,.}\,j\,\bm{)},R^{\prime}\bm{[}\,i^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,j^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ , where $R=r_{1}\cdots r_{n},R^{\prime}=r_{1^{\prime}}^{\prime}\cdots r_{n^{\prime}}^{\prime}$ are strings built from the right children of the central nodes.

This brings us to the visualization of $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{T},\mathbf{T}^{\prime})$ (under Assumption A) illustrated in Figure 1. Consider a $\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,(n+1)\,\bm{]}\times\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,(n^{\prime}+1)\,\bm{]}$ grid, and overlay on it the alignment graphs for string edit distance for $(L,L^{\prime})$ and $(R,R^{\prime})$ . Then, $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{T},\mathbf{T}^{\prime})$ can be visualized as two paths from $(1,1)$ to $(n+1,n^{\prime}+1)$ in the two respective alignment graphs. Whenever these paths intersect at a grid point $(i,i^{\prime})$ , $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{T},\mathbf{T}^{\prime})$ has the opportunity to map $c_{i}$ to $c_{i^{\prime}}^{\prime}$ , provided neither $c_{i}$ nor $c_{i^{\prime}}^{\prime}$ has been mapped previously.

Henceforth, we denote by $\mathsf{sim}((x,x^{\prime}),(y,y^{\prime}))$ the maximum value achievable by a sum of three terms:

- (1) the weight of a path from $(x,x^{\prime})$ to $(n+1,n^{\prime}+1)$ in the alignment graph of $\mathsf{sim}(L,L^{\prime})$ ;

- (2) the weight of a path from $(y,y^{\prime})$ to $(n+1,n^{\prime}+1)$ in the alignment graph of $\mathsf{sim}(R,R^{\prime})$ ; and

- (3) a sum of values of the form $\eta(c_{i},c_{i^{\prime}}^{\prime})$ for $(i,i^{\prime})$ where the two paths intersect, provided each $c_{i}$ and $c_{i^{\prime}}^{\prime}$ appears at most once.

By the previous discussion, $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{T},\mathbf{T}^{\prime})=\mathsf{sim}((1,1),(1,1))$ under Assumption A.

#### Reduction of caterpillar TED (under Assumption A) to APSP.

To compute $\mathsf{sim}((1,1),(1,1))$ , we utilize a divide-et-impera scheme. Given a rectangle in the grid defined by the lower-left corner $(a,a^{\prime})$ and the upper-right corner $(b,b^{\prime})$ , along with $\mathsf{sim}((x,x^{\prime}),(y,y^{\prime}))$ for all $(x,x^{\prime}),(y,y^{\prime})$ on the upper-right border of the rectangle, our task is to determine $\mathsf{sim}((x,x^{\prime}),(y,y^{\prime}))$ for all $(x,x^{\prime}),(y,y^{\prime})$ on the lower-left border of the rectangle. Note that computing the inputs becomes trivial when the rectangle we are considering is the whole grid.

*Figure 2: The figure illustrates an instance of the recursive scheme used to solve TED on caterpillars. The inputs can be visualized as fixing the starting points of the two paths on the upper right border (in orange) of the rectangle, and we are determining the maximum value achievable from there onwards. We are required to compute the same values for the lower left border (in purple). The divide-et-impera scheme divides the rectangle vertically into two smaller ones, parameterized by the corners $(a,a^{\prime}),(r,b^{\prime})$ and $(r,a^{\prime}),(b,b^{\prime})$ . The figure also demonstrates how to compute the inputs for the scheme on the left subrectangle for one specific case: one path leaves the upper border, and the other exits from the right border.*

Let $a<r<b$ . We split the rectangle vertically into two smaller rectangles (see Figure 2): one with corners $(a,a^{\prime})$ and $(r,b^{\prime})$ and the other with corners $(r,a^{\prime})$ and $(b,b^{\prime})$ . We aim to recurse on those two subrectangles.

For the right subrectangle, we can directly recurse since its inputs are a subset of those for the full rectangle.

For the left subrectangle, we must compute its input before recursing on it. First, let us consider $\mathsf{sim}((x,x^{\prime}),(y,y^{\prime}))$ for all $(x,x^{\prime})$ , $(y,y^{\prime})\in\bm{[}\,a\,\bm{.\,.}\,r\,\bm{]}\times b^{\prime}$ . These values corresponds to the case where both paths cross the upper border $\bm{[}\,a\,\bm{.\,.}\,r\,\bm{]}\times b^{\prime}$ in Figure 2. Note that these values are part of the input for the entire rectangle.

Similarly, when both paths cross the right border of the left subrectangle, i.e. $r\times\bm{[}\,a^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,b^{\prime}\,\bm{]}$ , no work needs to be done, as we can obtain the inputs from the right subrectangle’s output.

Next, suppose the path in $\mathsf{sim}(L,L^{\prime})$ crosses the upper border at $(x,b^{\prime})$ for some $x\in\bm{[}\,a\,\bm{.\,.}\,r\,\bm{]}$ , and the path in $\mathsf{sim}(R,R^{\prime})$ crosses the right border at $(r,y^{\prime})$ for some $y^{\prime}\in\bm{[}\,a^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,b^{\prime}\,\bm{]}$ . Then, we can decompose the path in $\mathsf{sim}(R,R^{\prime})$ into two parts (see Figure 2), as

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{sim}((x,b^{\prime}),(r,y^{\prime}))=\max_{(w,w^{\prime})\in(\bm{[}\,r\,\bm{.\,.}\,b\,\bm{]}\times b^{\prime})\cup(b\times\bm{[}\,a^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,b^{\prime}\,\bm{]})}\Big\{\ \mathsf{sim}(R\bm{[}\,r\,\bm{.\,.}\,w\,\bm{)},R^{\prime}\bm{[}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,w^{\prime}\,\bm{)})+\mathsf{sim}((x,b^{\prime}),(w,w^{\prime}))\ \Big\}. $$

In this maximization, the latter summands are part of the input for the full rectangle, and the former summands are border-to-border paths in an alignment graph which can be computed in time $\mathcal{O}(m^{2})$ , where $m=\max(b-a,b^{\prime}-a^{\prime})$ . Equation 1 can be computed concurrently for all such $x$ and $y^{\prime}$ via a max-plus product44 4 In max-plus products, the minimum operator is replaced by a maximum. Note that min and max products are equivalent, as one can be transformed into the other by appropriately reversing the signs of the matrices. For the remainder of this paper, we treat them as equivalent. in time $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(m))$ .

The case where the path in $\mathsf{sim}(L,L^{\prime})$ crosses the right border of the left subrectangle, and the the path in $\mathsf{sim}(R,R^{\prime})$ crosses the upper border of the left subrectangle can be handled symmetrically. This allows us now to recurse on the left subrectangle as well.

It remains to discuss how to patch together the outputs of the two subrectangles to get the outputs of the full rectangle. For the sake of brevity, we omit discussing this here, but it is not difficult to see that by employing similar calculations to those before (border-to-border paths in an alignment graph combined with the outputs of the two subrectangles via max-plus products), we can calculate $\mathsf{sim}((x,x^{\prime}),(y,y^{\prime}))$ for all $(x,x^{\prime}),(y,y^{\prime})$ on the lower-left border of the rectangle, ignoring the contribution arising from $c_{a}$ or $c_{a^{\prime}}^{\prime}$ being mapped to other central nodes. With some additional computations (which requires redefining $\mathsf{sim}((x,x^{\prime}),(y,y^{\prime}))$ to compute $2^{4}$ values instead of one, depending on whether central nodes $c_{a},c_{b},c_{a^{\prime}}^{\prime},c_{b^{\prime}}^{\prime}$ were already mapped or not), we can factor in these contributions and compute the desired output for the entire rectangle.

This shows how the divide-et-impera scheme can handle vertical cuts. By symmetry of the problem, the scheme can handle horizontal cuts as well, allowing us to split a single instance in four roughly equal parts to recurse on.

For a rough analysis, let us focus on the case when $n=n^{\prime}=2^{k}$ for which the scheme always recurses on squares. This results in the recurrence relation $\mathsf{T}(n)=4\cdot\mathsf{T}(n/2)+\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(n))$ , which implies $\mathsf{T}(n)=\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(n))$ .55 5 Here, we assume $\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(n)=\Omega(n^{2+\varepsilon})$ for some small $\varepsilon>0$ , a reasonable assumption given the widely accepted conjecture that no truly subcubic algorithms exist for MUL.

#### Getting rid of Assumption A.

Up to this point, we argued how to determine the similarity between two caterpillar trees, $\mathbf{T}$ and $\mathbf{T}^{\prime}$ , under Assumption A. In the general case, the mapping of $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{T},\mathbf{T}^{\prime})$ (when observed from the root downwards) preserves this assumption up to some point, i.e., there exist $a,b,a^{\prime},b^{\prime}$ such that nodes in $l_{1},\ldots,l_{a-1}$ are only mapped to nodes in $l_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,l_{a^{\prime}-1}^{\prime}$ , nodes in $r_{1},\ldots,r_{b-1}$ are only mapped to nodes in $r_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,r_{b^{\prime}-1}^{\prime}$ , nodes in $c_{1},\ldots,c_{\min(a,b)-1}$ are only mapped to nodes in $c_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,c_{\min(a^{\prime},b^{\prime})-1}^{\prime}$ . Then, one of two cases can occur:

- (a) $l_{a}$ is mapped to $c_{a^{\prime}}^{\prime}$ , nodes in $l_{a+1},\ldots,l_{b-1}$ are exclusively mapped to nodes $r_{a^{\prime}-1}^{\prime},\ldots,r_{b^{\prime}+1}^{\prime}$ , and $c_{b}$ is mapped to $r_{b^{\prime}}^{\prime}$ . The first and third conditions are optional; if they do not hold, we include $l_{a}$ , $r_{a^{\prime}}^{\prime}$ , and $l_{b}$ , $r_{b^{\prime}}^{\prime}$ , respectively, in the middle condition.

- (b) $r_{a}$ is mapped to $c_{a^{\prime}}^{\prime}$ , nodes in $r_{a-1},\ldots,r_{b+1}$ are mapped to nodes $l_{a^{\prime}+1}^{\prime},\ldots,l_{b^{\prime}-1}^{\prime}$ , and $c_{b}$ is mapped to $l_{b^{\prime}}^{\prime}$ . As before, the first and third conditions are optional; if they do not hold, we include $r_{a}$ , $r_{b}$ and $l_{a^{\prime}}^{\prime}$ , $l_{b^{\prime}}^{\prime}$ , respectively, in the middle condition.

Without loss of generality, we focus on the former case, as the two cases are symmetric.

*Figure 3: The general case for similarity mappings on caterpillar trees.*

This scenario is depicted in Figure 3 and can be visualized by overlaying an additional string similarity graph onto the existing ones in the grid (specifically, the one involved in $\mathsf{sim}(L,\mathsf{rev}(R^{\prime}))$ , where $\mathsf{rev}(R^{\prime})$ denotes the reversed string $R^{\prime}$ ). When overlaying this similarity graph, we ensure that the indices of $\mathsf{rev}(R^{\prime})$ align with the indexing of the grid, and the paths in this string alignment graph travel from the upper-left border to the lower-right border. The two paths that were previously observed now extend from $(1,1)$ to $(a,a^{\prime})$ and $(b,b^{\prime})$ , where $l_{a}$ is mapped to $c_{a^{\prime}}^{\prime}$ and $c_{b}$ is mapped to $l_{b^{\prime}}^{\prime}$ . Within this new alignment graph, we search for a path connecting $(a+1,a^{\prime})$ with $(b,b^{\prime}+1)$ . If $l_{a}$ is not mapped to $c_{a^{\prime}}^{\prime}$ or $c_{b}$ is not mapped to $l_{b^{\prime}}^{\prime}$ , then this path starts/ends at $(a,a^{\prime})$ and $(b,b^{\prime})$ , respectively.

The details necessary for considering this final path can be incorporated into the earlier divide-et-impera framework, although it necessitates additional inputs and outputs for the scheme. For the sake of brevity, we omit details here.

### 2.3 From TED on caterpillar trees to spine edit distance

#### Spine edit distance.

Our algorithm for TED on caterpillar trees generalizes to a problem known as Spine Edit Distance (SED), initially proposed in [BGHS19].

In SED, besides two forests $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ , we are provided with a spine for each forest. A spine $\mathbf{S}\subseteq\mathbf{F}$ is any root-to-leaf path within a forest (in cases where the forest contains multiple trees, the spine can start from any root of a tree contained in the forest). In SED we are given the similarity between all pairs of subtrees of $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ , provided at least one of the two roots does not lie on a spine. The task is to compute the similarity for all missing pairs of subtrees. Put more formally:

Spine Edit Distance (SED) Input: Two forests $\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ , two spines $\mathbf{S}\subseteq\mathbf{F},\mathbf{S}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ , and $\mathsf{sim}(\mathsf{sub}(v),\mathsf{sub}(v^{\prime}))$ for all $(v,v^{\prime})\in(\mathbf{F}\times\mathbf{F}^{\prime})\setminus(\mathbf{S}\times\mathbf{S}^{\prime})$ . Output: $\mathsf{sim}(\mathsf{sub}(v),\mathsf{sub}(v^{\prime}))$ for all $(v,v^{\prime})\in\mathbf{S}\times\mathbf{S}^{\prime}$ .

As already noticed in [BGHS19], TED can be reduced to SED by employing appropriate tree decompositions. In Section 6, we will prove the following:

#### Lemma 2.1.

Suppose there exists an algorithm for SED on two forests $\mathbf{H},\mathbf{H}^{\prime}$ running in time $\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{SED}}(m,m^{\prime})=\mathcal{O}(f(m)g(m^{\prime}))$ , where $m=|\mathbf{H}|,m^{\prime}=|\mathbf{H}^{\prime}|$ and $f(m)=\Omega(m),g(m^{\prime})=\Omega(m^{\prime})$ are some functions. Then, there is an algorithm for TED on two forests $\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ running in time $\mathcal{O}(f(n)g(n^{\prime})\log^{2}\max(n^{\prime},n))$ , where $n=|\mathbf{F}|,n^{\prime}=|\mathbf{F}^{\prime}|$ .

#### Reducing spine edit distance to APSP.

In the remaining part of this (sub)section, we describe the main ingredients we need to reduce SED to APSP.

We can assume, without loss of generality, that $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ are trees (by adding a virtual root and defining weights accordingly to enforce their deletion).

Let us further decompose $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ into $\mathbf{L},\mathbf{S},\mathbf{R}$ and $\mathbf{L}^{\prime},\mathbf{S}^{\prime},\mathbf{R}^{\prime}$ , where $\mathbf{R}$ is obtained from $\mathbf{F}$ by removing all nodes in $\mathbf{S}$ and those to the left of it. Similarly, $\mathbf{L}$ is obtained from $\mathbf{F}$ by removing all nodes in $\mathbf{S}$ and those to the right of it. We define $\mathbf{L}^{\prime}$ and $\mathbf{R}^{\prime}$ symmetrically. For simplicity, let us make a similar assumption as in the caterpillar case.

#### Assumption B.

For all $(v,v^{\prime})\in\mathbf{S}\times\mathbf{S}^{\prime}$ , nodes from $\mathbf{L},\mathbf{S}$ , and $\mathbf{R}$ are always only mapped by $\mathsf{sim}(\mathsf{sub}(v),\mathsf{sub}(v^{\prime}))$ to nodes of $\mathbf{L}^{\prime},\mathbf{S}^{\prime}$ , and $\mathbf{R}^{\prime}$ , respectively. \lipicsEnd

At this point, we can attempt to approach the problem similarly to how we did for caterpillar trees. Provided with the values $\mathsf{sim}(\mathsf{sub}(v),\mathsf{sub}(v^{\prime}))$ for all $(v,v^{\prime})\in(\mathbf{F}\times\mathbf{F}^{\prime})\setminus(\mathbf{S}\times\mathbf{S}^{\prime})$ in SED, we can construct the forest alignment graph of $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{L},\mathbf{L}^{\prime})$ and $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{R},\mathbf{R}^{\prime})$ , aiming to overlay them on top of each other. Refer to Figure 4 for a visualization and for some more (informal) discussion.

*Figure 4: To compute $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime})$ for the two depicted trees $\mathbf{T}$ and $\mathbf{T}^{\prime}$ under Assumption B, we can use the same visualization approach as before. Specifically, we overlay two tree alignment graphs corresponding to the concatenated left and right subtrees, tracing two paths that, whenever they intersect at two spine nodes, provide the possibility to map them. These graphs correspond to $L_{1}L_{2}\cdots L_{m}$ vs. $L_{1}^{\prime}L_{2}^{\prime}\cdots L^{\prime}_{m^{\prime}}$ and $\mathsf{rev}(R_{1}R_{2}\cdots R_{m})$ vs. $\mathsf{rev}(R_{1}^{\prime}R_{2}^{\prime}\cdots R^{\prime}_{m^{\prime}})$ , shown in blue and teal, respectively. Given the similarity values $\mathsf{sim}(\mathsf{sub}(v),\mathsf{sub}(v^{\prime}))$ for all $(v,v^{\prime})\in(\mathbf{F}\times\mathbf{F}^{\prime})\setminus(\mathbf{S}\times\mathbf{S}^{\prime})$ , we can construct these trees. In Spine Edit Distance (SED), instead of computing only $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime})$ , we also need to determine $\mathsf{sim}(\mathsf{sub}(s),\mathsf{sub}(s^{\prime}))$ for all $(s,s^{\prime})\in(\mathbf{S}\times\mathbf{S}^{\prime})$ . Fortunately, by employing a similar divide-and-conquer approach as used for caterpillars, computing $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime})$ naturally leads to obtaining these values as well. When designing such a divide-and-conquer scheme, the subproblems must be indexed by rectangles whose edges align with coordinates corresponding to spine nodes. This ensures that no diagonal edges in the tree alignment graphs “jump over” the sides of the rectangle, allowing for a “clean” partitioning into subproblems. As with caterpillar trees, removing Assumption B would introduce a third path between the two existing ones.*

However, this approach presents two challenges:

- • The two forest alignment graphs might have different grid sizes.

- • Identifying meeting points of paths in the two alignment graphs where nodes from $\mathbf{S}$ can be mapped to nodes of $\mathbf{S}^{\prime}$ is not as straightforward as for TED on caterpillar trees.

In Section 5, despite these challenges, we prove the following result: {mtheorem}[] Suppose there exists an algorithm computing the min-plus product of two $m\times m$ matrices in time $\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(m)$ . Then, there is an algorithm for SED running in time $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(n)+n^{2+o(1)})$ , where $n=\max(|\mathbf{F}|,|\mathbf{F}^{\prime}|)$ .

Observe that Section 2.3 together with Lemma 2.1 yields Section 1. Moreover, note that we establish not only the equivalence between TED and APSP, but also between SED and APSP.

Central to overcome the aforementioned challenges is the notation introduced by Mao in [Mao22]. This notation allows us to more directly formalize the problem in terms of forests, without relying on paths as an intermediary. Additionally, it leads to a more concise description of the divide-et-impera strategy that we employ to solve SED. However, this comes at the cost of obscuring the intuitive understanding provided by the two crossing paths, which remain essential for visualizing the structure of the problem.

#### Forest edit distance.

Generalizing TED on caterpillar trees on SED involves a shift from alignment graphs on strings to alignment graphs on forests. While there are algorithms finding border-to-border paths in the former in quadratic time, we still need to come up with an efficient way to compute such distances in the latter. The objective here is to develop either a truly subcubic algorithm or a reduction to APSP. We call the problem of finding border-to-border distances in a forest alignment graph the Forest Edit Distance problem (FED), and we present it here formulated using Mao’s notation (to be introduced in the next section).66 6 We remark that a different variant of FED was introduced already in [BGHS19]. There, it is defined with the same input, but the only required output is $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime})$ .

Before introducing FED, let us briefly introduce some notation and the bi-order traversal of a forest, already used in [Mao22]. The bi-order traversal of a forest $\mathbf{F}$ is a sequence of length $2\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert$ generated by starting a depth-first traversal from the virtual root, and adding a node to the sequence whenever we enter or leave a node. We then use $\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)}$ to denote the induced sub-forest of $\mathbf{F}$ consisting of nodes that appear twice in the segment $\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y-1\,\bm{]}$ in the bi-order traversal of $\mathbf{F}$ . For example $\mathbf{F}=\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,2\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert+1\,\bm{)}$ . For a node $v\in\mathbf{F}$ , we let $\mathsf{l}(v)$ denote the first occurrence of $v$ in the bi-order traversal of $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathsf{r}(v)$ denote one plus the last occurrence of $v$ .

Forest Edit Distance (FED) Input: Two forests $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ and $\mathsf{sim}(\mathsf{sub}(v),\mathsf{sub}(v^{\prime}))$ for all $(v,v^{\prime})\in\mathbf{F}\times\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ . Output: The following values: • $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime})$ for all $x,y\in\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,(2|\mathbf{F}|+1)\,\bm{]}$ , • $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,(2|\mathbf{F}|+1)\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ for all $x\in\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,(2|\mathbf{F}|+1)\,\bm{]},y^{\prime}\in\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,(2|\mathbf{F}^{\prime}|+1)\,\bm{]}$ , • $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ for all $x^{\prime},y^{\prime}\in\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,(2|\mathbf{F}^{\prime}|+1)\,\bm{]}$ , and • $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,(2|\mathbf{F}|+1)\,\bm{)})$ for all $y\in\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,(2|\mathbf{F}|+1)\,\bm{]},x^{\prime}\in\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,(2|\mathbf{F}^{\prime}|+1)\,\bm{]}$ .

In Section 4, we demonstrate that FED can indeed be reduced to APSP, and we prove:

[] Suppose there exists an algorithm computing the min-plus product of two $m\times m$ matrices in time $\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(m)$ . Then, there is an algorithm for FED running in time $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(n)+n^{2+o(1)})$ , where $n=\max(|\mathbf{F}|,|\mathbf{F}^{\prime}|)$ .

To address FED, we adopt a divide-et-impera approach. Our recursive scheme presented in Section 2.3 builds upon Mao’s decomposition scheme for forests introduced in [Mao22].

### 2.4 Unweighted Tree Edit Distance

We now discuss our algorithm for Unweighted Tree Edit Distance. Consider two forests $\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ with $n,n^{\prime}$ nodes respectively. We can make two simple observations with respect to the matrices involved in max-plus products in our reduction:

- • The similarity matrices are row-monotone and column-monotone.

- • The entries of the similarity matrices are bounded by $\mathcal{O}(\min(n,n^{\prime}))$ .

Note that the first observation holds even in the weighted setting. For example, in Equation (1), for a fixed $x$ , $\mathsf{sim}((x,b^{\prime}),(r,y^{\prime}))$ must be non-decreasing in $y^{\prime}$ . In the unweighted setting, the second observation additionally holds, since the value of any alignment is at most twice the number of nodes. In particular, in computing FED (Section 2.3) and SED (Section 2.3), we can instead use Bounded Monotone Min-Plus Matrix Multiplication.

Recall that the min-plus (or max-plus) product of an $n\times n$ arbitrary integer matrix and an $n\times n$ bounded monotone matrix can be computed in time $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{(3+\omega)/2})$ [CDXZ22], with subsequent generalizations to arbitrary rectangular matrices [Dür23, SY24].

Directly applying the observation, we have that SED between two forests of size $m,m^{\prime}$ can be computed in time $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\max(m,m^{\prime})^{(3+\omega)/2})$ [CDXZ22] which may be improved to $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{\min(m,m^{\prime})}\cdot\max(m,m^{\prime})^{(2+\omega)/2})$ by our bound on entries [Dür23].

Let us see the result we can obtain via Lemma 2.1.

Recall that Lemma 2.1 states that given an $\mathcal{O}(f(m)g(m^{\prime}))$ algorithm for SED, there is an $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(f(n)g(n^{\prime}))$ algorithm for TED on two forests of size $n,n^{\prime}$ . Suppose $f(x)=\mathcal{O}(x^{a}),g(x)=\mathcal{O}(x^{b})$ . Setting $m^{\prime}=1$ , we have $m^{(2+\omega)/2}=\mathcal{O}(m^{a}m^{\prime b})=\mathcal{O}(m^{a})$ , so that $a\geq(2+\omega)/2$ . Similarly, we obtain $b\geq(2+\omega)/2$ , so that we only obtain a TED algorithm running in time $\mathcal{O}(n^{2+\omega})$ for two forests of size $n$ . Even if $\omega=2$ , the running time $\mathcal{O}(n^{4})$ is prohibitively expensive.

In general, a running time $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\min(m,m^{\prime})^{c}\max(m,m^{\prime})^{d})$ can be upper bounded by $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(m^{\max(c,d)}m^{\prime d})$ . Hence, in order to keep the total exponents of the two formulations the same, we hope to obtain a running time with $c\geq d$ without increasing $c+d$ , i.e., we hope for an algorithm for SED with running time $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\min(m,m^{\prime})^{c}\max(m,m^{\prime})^{d})$ for $c\geq d$ and $c+d=(3+\omega)/2$ . This is achieved by the following theorem:

#### Theorem 2.2.

There is an $(n/n^{\prime})^{1+o(1)}\cdot\left(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(n^{\prime})+n^{\prime 2+o(1)}g(n^{\prime})\right)$ algorithm for unweighted SED, where $n=\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert,n^{\prime}=\left\lvert\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\right\rvert$ , $n\geq n^{\prime}$ , and $\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(n^{\prime},n^{\prime},n^{\prime},\mathrm{D})=\mathcal{O}(f(n^{\prime})g(\mathrm{D}))$ for some functions $f,g$ .

We now illustrate the techniques required to obtain the above result. Suppose we have two trees $\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ of size $n,n^{\prime}$ with spines $\mathbf{S}=\{r,\cdots,q\},\mathbf{S}^{\prime}=\{r^{\prime},\cdots,q^{\prime}\}$ . Assume without loss of generality that $n\gg n^{\prime}$ . For simplicity, we again assume Assumption B.

We can formulate the SED problem using a divide-et-impera scheme. Since $n\gg n^{\prime}$ , we only decompose the larger tree $\mathbf{F}$ . For a given threshold $\gamma$ , we can efficiently find a subsequence of spine vertices $I=\bm{[}\,s_{1}\,\bm{.\,.}\,s_{d}\,\bm{]}$ with $r=s_{1},q=s_{d}$ such that for all $i<d$ , either $\left\lvert\mathsf{sub}(s_{i})\setminus\mathsf{sub}(s_{i+1})\right\rvert\leq\gamma$ or $s_{i}$ immediately precedes $s_{i+1}$ in $\mathbf{S}$ .

We can then compute SED recursively in a bottom-up manner. We begin by computing $\mathsf{sim}(\mathsf{sub}(s_{d}),\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ for all $x^{\prime},y^{\prime}\in\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,2\left\lvert\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\right\rvert+1\,\bm{)}$ . Since $\mathsf{sub}(s_{d})$ is a single node, we can compute this efficiently. Next, for $i<d$ , given $\mathsf{sim}(\mathsf{sub}(s_{i+1}),\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ for all $x^{\prime},y^{\prime}$ , our hope is to compute $\mathsf{sim}(\mathsf{sub}(s_{i}),\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ for all $x^{\prime},y^{\prime}$ . First, suppose $\left\lvert\mathsf{sub}(s_{i})\setminus\mathsf{sub}(s_{i+1})\right\rvert\leq\gamma$ . In this case we recurse on the smaller problem of size $(\gamma,n^{\prime})$ . Since there are at most $3n/\gamma$ sub-problems in $I$ , the total time on the first case is

$$ \mathsf{T}(n,n^{\prime})=(3n/\gamma)\cdot\mathsf{T}(\gamma,n^{\prime}) $$

which yields total time $(n/n^{\prime})^{1+o(1)}\cdot n^{\prime(3+\omega)/2}$ , since when $\gamma=\mathcal{O}(n^{\prime})$ , we apply the recursive scheme employed in Section 2.3 in time $n^{\prime(3+\omega)/2}$ .

Thus, it remains to handle the case where $s_{i}$ immediately precedes $s_{i+1}$ . Under Assumption B, we can decompose the similarity when $s_{i}$ is not aligned as follows:

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{sim}(\mathsf{sub}(s_{i}),\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})=\max\nolimits_{\begin{subarray}{c}w^{\prime}\in\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(r^{\prime})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(q^{\prime})\,\bm{]}\\
z^{\prime}\in\bm{[}\,\mathsf{r}(q^{\prime})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(r^{\prime})\,\bm{]}\end{subarray}}\Big\{\  \displaystyle\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(s_{i})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(s_{i+1})\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,w^{\prime}\,\bm{)}) \displaystyle+\mathsf{sim}(\mathsf{sub}(s_{i+1}),\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,w^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,z^{\prime}\,\bm{)}) \displaystyle+\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{r}(s_{i+1})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(s_{i})\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,z^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})\ \Big\}. $$

To handle the case where $s_{i}$ is aligned, say to vertex $v$ , we can add $\eta(s_{i},v)$ to the value of $\mathsf{sim}(\mathsf{sub}(s_{i}),\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(v)+1\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(v)\,\bm{)})$ . For completeness, we also ensure monotonicity after updating the values in a post-processing step (i.e. $\mathsf{sim}(\mathsf{sub}(s_{i}),\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})\geq\mathsf{sub}(s_{i},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(v)\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(v)\,\bm{)})$ if $x^{\prime}\preceq\mathsf{l}(v)\prec\mathsf{r}(v)\preceq y^{\prime}$ ). The computation can be written as a max-plus product of three $\mathcal{O}(n^{\prime})\times\mathcal{O}(n^{\prime})$ matrices with entries bounded by $\mathcal{O}(n^{\prime})$ since each entry is a similarity measure between two forests, one of size at most $\mathcal{O}(n^{\prime})$ . Since the matrices are also monotone, the summands can be combined in time $\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(n^{\prime})=\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{\prime(3+\omega)/2})$ .

*Figure 5: The alignment whose value is computed in Equation 2 visualized as a Border-to-Border (BBD) distance computation. The value of the orange path corresponds to the first summand, or the alignment between $\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(s_{i})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(s_{i+1}\,\bm{)}$ and $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,w^{\prime}\,\bm{)}$ . The value of the blue path corresponds to the last summand, or the alignment between $\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{r}(s_{i+1})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(s_{i}\,\bm{)}$ and $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,z^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)}$ . For every pair of points on the right border, we have the optimal alignment between $\mathsf{sub}(s_{i+1})$ and $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,w^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,z^{\prime}\,\bm{)}$ .*

The second summand is available to us as part of the bottom-up recursion. It remains to compute the first and last summand. Consider the first summand. Observe that it is exactly the third output of FED between $\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(s_{i})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(s_{i+1})\,\bm{)}$ and $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(r^{\prime})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(q^{\prime})\,\bm{)}$ . Similarly, the third summand is exactly the third output of FED between $\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{r}(s_{i+1})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(s_{i})\,\bm{)}$ and $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{r}(q^{\prime})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(r^{\prime})\,\bm{)}$ . Since none of the forests contain any spine nodes $\mathbf{S},\mathbf{S}^{\prime}$ , all inputs to the FED instances are given by the inputs of the SED instance.

Our goal is now to compute these two FED instances. We can bound the size of $\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(s_{i})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(s_{i+1})\,\bm{)}$ and $\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{r}(s_{i+1})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(s_{i})\,\bm{)}$ by $\left\lvert\mathsf{sub}(s_{i})\setminus\mathsf{sub}(s_{i+1})\right\rvert$ . However, it is possible that $\left\lvert\mathsf{sub}(s_{i})\setminus\mathsf{sub}(s_{i+1})\right\rvert=\Theta(n)$ , in which case directly applying Section 2.3 on the FED instance already takes $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(n))$ time in this one step alone. Even if the entries are bounded by $\mathcal{O}(n^{\prime})$ , the output of FED instance is already size $\Omega(n^{2})$ . How can we reduce the dependence on $n$ ? In our SED application, we have only used the third output of FED. In fact, we show that all outputs except the first output (which has size $\Omega(n^{2})$ ) can be computed efficiently. Formally, we define the Unbalanced Forest Edit Distance (UFED) problem as computing all but the first output of FED and show the following theorem.

#### Theorem 2.3.

There is an algorithm for unweighted UFED running in time $(n/n^{\prime})^{1+o(1)}\cdot\left(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(n^{\prime})+n^{\prime 2+o(1)}g(n^{\prime})\right)$ where $n=\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert$ , $n^{\prime}=\left\lvert\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\right\rvert$ , $n\geq n^{\prime}$ and $\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(n^{\prime},n^{\prime},n^{\prime},\mathrm{D})=\mathcal{O}(f(n^{\prime})g(\mathrm{D}))$ for some functions $f,g$ .

In the remainder of the technical overview of the unweighted algorithm, we give an overview of the proof of Theorem 2.3. Further simplifying under Assumption B, our previous discussion shows that it is enough to only compute the third FED output. To this end, consider the alignment graph $\bar{\mathbf{G}}$ of two forests $\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ with vertices $\mathbf{F}\times\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ arranged in a grid where both trees are ordered in pre-order traversal.

The grid contains horizontal and vertical edges of weight $0$ (corresponding to vertex deletions) and edges from $(v,v^{\prime})$ to $(w,w^{\prime})$ of weight $\mathsf{sim}(\mathsf{sub}(v),\mathsf{sub}(v^{\prime}))$ where $w$ (resp. $w^{\prime}$ ) is the first vertex after $\mathsf{sub}(v)$ (resp. $\mathsf{sub}(v^{\prime})$ ) in pre-order traversal i.e. the first vertices that can be aligned after aligning $\mathsf{sub}(v)$ and $\mathsf{sub}(v^{\prime})$ . The desired output of FED then corresponds to computing all distances from the left border to the right border of the grid. In contrast, the general FED problem asks to compute all distances from the left and bottom borders to the right and top borders.

The alignment graph $\mathbf{G}$ has dimension $n\times n^{\prime}$ , so ideally we hope to be able to breaking the it into $\mathcal{O}(n/n^{\prime})$ subgraphs, each of size $\mathcal{O}(n^{\prime})\times\mathcal{O}(n^{\prime})$ . Then, we can compute FED on each subgraph and combine the results using $\mathcal{O}(n/n^{\prime})$ bounded monotone max-plus products, thus computing the desired FED output in total time $\mathcal{O}((n/n^{\prime})\cdot\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(n^{\prime}))$ . However, in reality, it is not simple to decompose $\mathbf{G}$ to $\mathcal{O}(n/n^{\prime})$ subgraphs and combine the results, as there can be edges connecting two nodes that are far away in the alignment graph. Hence, in our actual algorithm, we apply a divide-et-impera scheme utilizing Mao’s tree decomposition [Mao22], which incurs an additional $(n/n^{\prime})^{o(1)}$ factor. Still, we obtain the desired almost-linear dependence on the size of the larger forest $n=\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert$ . In particular, at least under Assumption B, both FED and SED can be computed in time $\mathcal{O}(\min(m,m^{\prime})^{(1+\omega)/2}\max(m,m^{\prime})^{1+o(1)})$ .

To remove Assumption B, we must be able to additionally compute distances from the left border to the top border in BBD instances, corresponding to the second and fourth outputs of the FED problem (see Section 4.6). In the SED instance we then proceed by careful case analysis to ensure that we consider all possible alignments between the two forests (see Section 5.5). Applying Lemma 2.1 then yields an $n^{1+o(1)}n^{\prime(1+\omega)/2}$ -time algorithm for unweighted tree edit distance between forests of size $n,n^{\prime}$ and $n\geq n^{\prime}$ , proving Corollary 1.2.

### 2.5 Organization of the paper

The structure of this paper is as follows. In Section 3, we introduce the remaining notation not covered in this section. Next, in Section 4, we present an algorithm for computing border-to-border distances in forest alignment graphs within APSP time. With this algorithm in hand, we extend the caterpillar algorithm to the SED problem in Section 5, where we shift from a path-based approach to more formal and concise notation, offering a clearer treatment of the problem. Both Section 4 and Section 5 are structured to first discuss complexity in terms of the larger of the two input forests which is optimal when forests are similar in size. In the second part of these sections, we provide a more detailed analysis suited for unbalanced cases by parameterizing the complexity by both forest sizes. In these sections, we provide algorithms for both weighted and unweighted TED, in particular noting when the unweighted TED problem can be computed more efficiently. In Section 6, we show how to solve TED using SED, providing a generic reduction for both weighted and unweighted TED, thus completing the proofs in this paper.

## 3 Preliminaries

#### Set notation.

For integers $i,j\in\mathbb{Z}$ , we use the notation $\bm{[}\,i\,\bm{.\,.}\,j\,\bm{]}$ to represent the set $\{i,\dots,j\}$ , and $\bm{[}\,i\,\bm{.\,.}\,j\,\bm{)}$ to denote the set $\{i,\dots,j-1\}$ . We define $\bm{(}\,i\,\bm{.\,.}\,j\,\bm{]}$ and $\bm{(}\,i\,\bm{.\,.}\,j\,\bm{)}$ similarly.

Consider the infinite grid $\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}$ , and consider a subset of the form of a rectangle $\bm{[}\,a\,\bm{.\,.}\,b\,\bm{]}\times\bm{[}\,a^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,b^{\prime}\,\bm{]}$ for some $a,b,a^{\prime},b^{\prime}$ . We define $\mathsf{B}^{\bot}(a,a^{\prime},b,b^{\prime})$ and $\mathsf{B}^{\top}(a,a^{\prime},b,b^{\prime})$ to be set of grid points located at the bottom-left and upper-right border of such rectangle $\bm{[}\,a\,\bm{.\,.}\,b\,\bm{]}\times\bm{[}\,a^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,b^{\prime}\,\bm{]}$ . Put more formally:

#### Definition 3.1.

For integers $a,a^{\prime},b,b^{\prime}$ we define

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{B}^{\top}(a,a^{\prime},b,b^{\prime}) \displaystyle\coloneqq(\{b\}\times\bm{[}\,a^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,b^{\prime}\,\bm{]})\cup(\bm{[}\,a\,\bm{.\,.}\,b\,\bm{]}\times\{b^{\prime}\}),\text{ and } \displaystyle\mathsf{B}^{\bot}(a,a^{\prime},b,b^{\prime}) \displaystyle\coloneqq(\{a\}\times\bm{[}\,a^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,b^{\prime}\,\bm{]})\cup(\bm{[}\,a\,\bm{.\,.}\,b\,\bm{]}\times\{a^{\prime}\}). $$

#### Notation on ordered trees.

For consistency, we adopt most of the notations for TED from [Mao22].

In TED we work with ordered trees. For a tree $\mathbf{T}$ , we denote its root as $\mathsf{root}(\mathbf{T})$ . We also treat a forest $\mathbf{F}$ as ordered, meaning that the sequence of trees within the forest is relevant. In this context, we can view a forest $\mathbf{F}$ as a tree with a virtual root, whose children are the roots of the trees in $\mathbf{F}$ , ordered from left to right as they appear in the forest.

For a tree $\mathbf{T}\in\mathbf{F}$ , let $\mathbf{F}\setminus\mathbf{T}$ represent the forest obtained by removing $\mathbf{T}$ from $\mathbf{F}$ while preserving the order of the remaining trees. We use $\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert$ to denote the number of nodes in $\mathbf{F}$ . Occasionally, we may also abuse notation by using $\mathbf{F}$ to refer to the set of nodes in the forest, though the context will make this clear. For two forests $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ , we denote their concatenation (from left to right) as $\mathbf{F}+\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ . An empty forest is denoted by $\varnothing$ . For a node $v\in\mathbf{F}$ , we let $\mathsf{sub}(v)$ represent the subtree rooted at $v$ .

Finally, we write $\mathsf{rev}(\mathbf{F})$ for the reversed forests of $\mathbf{F}$ , obtained by taking each node of $\mathbf{F}$ (including its virtual root), and reversing the order of the children.

#### Bi-order traversal.

To compute the similarity between forests, we use the notation introduced by [Mao22], which allows us to conveniently index subforests of $\mathbf{F}$ and express calculations in a way that is well-suited to max-plus products.

#### Definition 3.2 ([Mao22, Definition 2.3]).

Consider the depth-first traversal of a forest $\mathbf{F}$ starting from the virtual root, with subtrees recursively traversed from left to right. From that we can generate an bi-order traversal sequence of length $2\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert$ , where each node appears twice, in the following way:

- • Start from the empty sequence.

- • Every time we enter or leave a node, we attach the node to the end of the sequence (do not attach the virtual root).

We use $\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,i\,\bm{]}$ to denote the $i$ -th node in such sequence.

Observe that bi-order traversal of $\mathsf{rev}(\mathbf{F})$ corresponds to the reversed bi-order traversal of $\mathbf{F}$ .

#### Definition 3.3 ([Mao22, Definition 2.4]).

For $1\leq\ell\leq r\leq 2\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert+1$ , consider bi-order traversal $\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{]},\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,2\,\bm{]},\ldots,\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,2\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert\,\bm{]}$ of $\mathbf{F}$ . We use $\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\ell\,\bm{.\,.}\,r\,\bm{)}$ to denote the forest obtained by removing from $\mathbf{F}$ all nodes that appear at least once in $\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{]},\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,2\,\bm{]},\ldots,\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\ell-1\,\bm{]}$ or $\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,r\,\bm{]},\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,r+1\,\bm{]},\ldots,\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,2\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert\,\bm{]}$ , and we call such forest a subforest of $\mathbf{F}$ .

Consider the bi-order traversal sequence of a forest $\mathbf{F}$ . For a node $v\in\mathbf{F}$ , we define $\mathsf{l}(v)$ as the first index where $v$ appears in the bi-order traversal sequence, and $\mathsf{r}(v)$ as one plus the second index where $v$ appears. By these definitions, $\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\ell\,\bm{.\,.}\,r\,\bm{)}$ contains $v$ if and only if $\ell\leq\mathsf{l}(v)$ and $\mathsf{r}(v)\leq r$ . Additionally, $\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(v)\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(v)\,\bm{)}$ corresponds to $\mathsf{sub}(v)$ . Note that $\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\ell\,\bm{.\,.}\,r\,\bm{)}$ and $\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\ell^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,r^{\prime}\,\bm{)}$ may represent the same forest for distinct pairs $(\ell,r)$ and $(\ell^{\prime},r^{\prime})$ .

#### Definition 3.4 ([Mao22, Definition 2.5]).

For a forest $\mathbf{F}$ , we say subforest $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ of $\mathbf{F}$ is a synchronous subforest of $\mathbf{F}$ if there exists a node $v\in\mathbf{F}$ that is either a node in $\mathbf{F}$ or the virtual root of $\mathbf{F}$ , and such that $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ is the union of subtrees of subsequent children of $v$ .

#### Anchors and anchor sets.

A key point in working with a similarity of the form $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ between two subforests $\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)}$ and $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)}$ in bi-order traversal is realizing that the following inequality holds for all $(z,z^{\prime})\in\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{]}\times\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{]}$ :

$$ \mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})\geq\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,z\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,z^{\prime}\,\bm{)})+\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,z\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,z^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)}). $$

An anchor, is a pair $(z,z^{\prime})$ where such last inequality holds with equality.

#### Definition 3.5 (Anchors and anchor sets).

Let $\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ be two forests, and let $\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)}$ be two subforests. We say that $(z,z^{\prime})\in\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,(2|\mathbf{F}|+1)\,\bm{]}\times\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,(2|\mathbf{F}^{\prime}|+1)\,\bm{]}$ is an anchor of $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ if $x\leq z\leq y$ , and $x^{\prime}\leq z^{\prime}\leq y^{\prime}$ and

$$ \mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})=\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,z\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,z^{\prime}\,\bm{)})+\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,z\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,z^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)}). $$

Further, we say $\mathsf{B}\subseteq\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,(2|\mathbf{F}|+1)\,\bm{]}\times\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,(2|\mathbf{F}^{\prime}|+1)\,\bm{]}$ is an anchor set of $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ if there exists $(z,z^{\prime})\in\mathsf{B}$ such that $(z,z^{\prime})$ is an anchor of $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ .

We note that we use the concept of anchor sets, defined as subsets of $\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,(2|\mathbf{F}|+1)\,\bm{]}\times\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,(2|\mathbf{F}^{\prime}|+1)\,\bm{]}$ , not only for similarities of the form $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ but also for other subforests where the same bi-order indexing applies, such as $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,z\,\bm{)}+\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,z\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ .

We extend the concept of anchors to paired anchors.

#### Definition 3.6 (Paired anchors and anchor sets).

Let $\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ be two forests, and let $\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)}$ be two subforests. We say that $(z,z^{\prime}),(w,w^{\prime})\in\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,(2|\mathbf{F}|+1)\,\bm{]}\times\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,(2|\mathbf{F}^{\prime}|+1)\,\bm{]}$ are paired anchors of $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ if $x\leq z\leq w\leq y$ , and $x^{\prime}\leq z^{\prime}\leq w^{\prime}\leq y^{\prime}$ and

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)}) \displaystyle=\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,z\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,z^{\prime}\,\bm{)}) \displaystyle+\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,z\,\bm{.\,.}\,w\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,z^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,w^{\prime}\,\bm{)})+\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,w\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,w^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)}). $$

Further, we say $\mathsf{B},\mathsf{B}^{\prime}\subseteq\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,(2|\mathbf{F}|+1)\,\bm{]}\times\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,(2|\mathbf{F}^{\prime}|+1)\,\bm{]}$ are paired anchor sets of $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ if there are $(z,z)\in\mathsf{B}$ and $(w,w^{\prime})\in\mathsf{B}^{\prime}$ such that $(z,z^{\prime})$ and $(w,w^{\prime})$ are paired anchors.

Observe that a set $\mathsf{B}$ is an anchor set of $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ if and only if

$$ \mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})=\max_{(z,z^{\prime})\in\mathsf{B}:x\leq z\leq y,x^{\prime}\leq z^{\prime}\leq y^{\prime}}\Big\{\ \mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,z\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,z^{\prime}\,\bm{)})\ +\ \mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,z\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,z^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})\ \Big\}. $$

Moreover, for sets $\mathsf{B}$ and $\mathsf{B}^{\prime}$ are paired anchor sets holds

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})=\max\nolimits_{\begin{subarray}{c}(z,z^{\prime})\in\mathsf{B}:x\leq z\leq y,x^{\prime}\leq z^{\prime}\leq y^{\prime}\\
(w,w^{\prime})\in\mathsf{B}^{\prime}:z\leq w\leq y,z^{\prime}\leq y^{\prime}\leq y^{\prime}\end{subarray}} \displaystyle\Big\{\ \mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,z\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,z^{\prime}\,\bm{)}) \displaystyle+\ \mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,z\,\bm{.\,.}\,w\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,z^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,w^{\prime}\,\bm{)}) \displaystyle+\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,w\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,w^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})\ \Big\}. $$

In previous works, such as [Mao22, Equation (9)], it was observed that when $\mathbf{F}$ consists of more than one tree, there exists an anchor set with a simple representation. More specifically, if we can write $\mathbf{F}=\mathbf{F}_{\mathsf{l}}+\mathbf{F}_{\mathsf{r}}$ for two forests $\mathbf{F}_{\mathsf{l}},\mathbf{F}_{\mathsf{r}}$ , then $(2|\mathbf{F}_{\mathsf{l}}|+1)\times\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,(2|\mathbf{F}^{\prime}|+1)\,\bm{]}$ is an anchor set of $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime})$ . We rephrase this observation for subforests as follows.

#### Proposition 3.7.

Suppose that for two subforests $\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)}$ and some $z\in\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{]}$ , we have that $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})=\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,z\,\bm{)}+\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,z\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ holds. Then, $z\times\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,(2\left\lvert\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\right\rvert+1)\,\bm{]}$ is an anchor set of $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ . \lipicsEnd

Next, we prove Proposition 3.8 that allows us to transform anchor sets.

#### Proposition 3.8.

Let $(z,z^{\prime})$ be an anchor of $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ . Suppose $\mathsf{B}$ is an anchor set of $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,z\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,z^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ . Then, the two following hold:

- (i) For any anchor set $\mathsf{A}$ such that $(z,z^{\prime})\in\mathsf{A}$ , we have that $\mathsf{A}$ and $\mathsf{B}$ are paired anchor set.

- (ii) $\mathsf{B}$ is also anchor set of $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ .

#### Proof 3.9.

From the assumptions on $\mathsf{B}$ , there exists $(w,w^{\prime})\in\mathsf{B}$ such that $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,z\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,z^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})=\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,z\,\bm{.\,.}\,w\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,z^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,w^{\prime}\,\bm{)})+\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,w\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,w^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ . Combining this with the anchor assumption on $(z,z^{\prime})$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)}) \displaystyle=\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,z\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,z^{\prime}\,\bm{)})+\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,z\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,z^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)}) \displaystyle=\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,z\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,z^{\prime}\,\bm{)})+\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,z\,\bm{.\,.}\,w\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,z^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,w^{\prime}\,\bm{)})+\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,w\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,w^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)}). $$

This shows (i). To prove (ii), it suffices to show that $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,w\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,w^{\prime}\,\bm{)})=\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,z\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,z^{\prime}\,\bm{)})+\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,z\,\bm{.\,.}\,w\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,z^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,w^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ , which would imply that $(w,w^{\prime})$ is an anchor of $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ . To this end, observe that $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,w\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,w^{\prime}\,\bm{)})>\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,z\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,z^{\prime}\,\bm{)})+\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,z\,\bm{.\,.}\,w\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,z^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,w^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ would imply

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)}) \displaystyle=\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,z\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,z^{\prime}\,\bm{)})+\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,z\,\bm{.\,.}\,w\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,z^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,w^{\prime}\,\bm{)})+\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,w\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,w^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)}) \displaystyle<\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,w\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,w^{\prime}\,\bm{)})+\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,w\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,w^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)}) \displaystyle\leq\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)}), $$

a contradiction.

Using Proposition 3.8 we can transform the anchor set from Proposition 3.7 as follows.

#### Proposition 3.10.

Consider two subforests $\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)}$ , and suppose there exist $v\in\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)}$ and $v^{\prime}\in\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)}$ such that

$$ \mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})=\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(v)\,\bm{)}+\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(v)\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(v^{\prime})\,\bm{)})+\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(v^{\prime})\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)}). $$

Then, we have that

$$ \mathsf{B}^{\top}(1,1,\mathsf{l}(v),\mathsf{l}(v^{\prime}))\ =\ (\mathsf{l}(v)\times\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(v^{\prime})\,\bm{]})\ \cup\ (\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(v)\,\bm{]}\times\mathsf{l}(v^{\prime})) $$

is an anchor set of $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ .

#### Proof 3.11.

By Proposition 3.7, the set $\mathsf{B}\coloneqq\mathsf{l}(v)\times\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,(2\left\lvert\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\right\rvert+1)\,\bm{]}$ serves as an anchor set for $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(v)\,\bm{)}+\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(v)\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(v^{\prime})\,\bm{)}+\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(v^{\prime})\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ .

Now, we perform a case distinction on whether there is an anchor $(z,z^{\prime})\in\mathsf{B}$ of $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(v)\,\bm{)}+\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(v)\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(v^{\prime})\,\bm{)})+\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(v^{\prime})\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ contained in the subset $\mathsf{B}^{\prime}$ or not. For certain of forms of similiarities we can also find paired anchor sets.

#### Proposition 3.12.

Let $\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ be two forests, and let $\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)}$ be two subforests. Then, the two following hold:

- (ii) For any $v\in\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)}$ and $v^{\prime}\in\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)}$ such that $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})=\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(v)\,\bm{)}+\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(v)\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(v^{\prime})\,\bm{)})+\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(v^{\prime})\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ , we have that $\mathsf{B}^{\top}(1,1,\mathsf{l}(v),\mathsf{l}(v^{\prime}))$ and $\mathsf{B}^{\bot}(\mathsf{r}(v),\mathsf{r}(v^{\prime}),2\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert+1,2\left\lvert\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\right\rvert+1)$ are paired anchors sets of $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ .

#### Proof 3.13.

We first prove (i). By Proposition 3.7, we have that $\mathsf{l}(v)\times\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,(2|\mathbf{F}^{\prime}|+1)\,\bm{]}$ is an anchor set of $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ . Observe that $\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(v)\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)}=\mathsf{sub}(v)+\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{r}(v)\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)}$ . Thus, by Proposition 3.7, for every $(z,z^{\prime})\in\mathsf{l}(v)\times\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,(2|\mathbf{F}^{\prime}|+1)\,\bm{]}$ , we have that $\mathsf{r}(v)\times\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,(2|\mathbf{F}^{\prime}|+1)\,\bm{]}$ is an anchor set of $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,z\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,z^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ .
