For each $(z,z^{\prime})\in\mathsf{B}^{\top}(1,1,\mathsf{l}(v),\mathsf{l}(v^{\prime}))$ , we have $\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,z\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)}=\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,z\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(v)\,\bm{)}+\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{r}(v)\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)}$ and $\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,z^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)}=\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,z^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(v^{\prime})\,\bm{)}+\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{r}(v^{\prime})\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)}$ . Thus, we can once again apply Proposition 3.10, using a symmetric equivalent that uses $\mathsf{r}(v)$ instead of $\mathsf{l}(v)$ , and subsequently apply Proposition 3.8(i).

#### Aligned Subtrees.

Next, we introduced what means for two subtrees to be aligned by a similarity.

#### Definition 3.14.

Given two forests $\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ and nodes $v\in\mathbf{F}$ , $v^{\prime}\in\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ , we say $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime})$ aligns $\mathsf{sub}(v)$ to $\mathsf{sub}(v^{\prime})$ if

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}) \displaystyle=\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(v)\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(v^{\prime})\,\bm{)})+\mathsf{sim}(\mathsf{sub}(v),\mathsf{sub}(v^{\prime})) \displaystyle+\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{r}(v)\,\bm{.\,.}\,(2\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert+1)\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{r}(v^{\prime})\,\bm{.\,.}\,(2\left\lvert\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\right\rvert+1)\,\bm{)}). $$

In other words, $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime})$ aligns $\mathsf{sub}(v)$ to $\mathsf{sub}(v^{\prime})$ , if $\{(\mathsf{l}(v),\mathsf{l}(v))\},\{(\mathsf{r}(v),\mathsf{r}(v^{\prime}))\}$ are paired anchor sets.

#### Proposition 3.15.

Given two forests $\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ and a node $v\in\mathbf{F}$ , let $\mathbf{P}$ be the set of nodes contained in the path going from the virtual root of $\mathbf{F}$ to $v$ (virtual root and $v$ excluded). Then, for each pair of subforests $\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)}$ and $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)}$ such that $\mathsf{sub}(v)\subseteq\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)}$ at least one of the two following cases holds:

- (a) There exists a node $u\in\mathbf{P}$ such that $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ aligns $\mathsf{sub}(u)$ to a subtree of $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ .

- (b) $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})=\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(v)\,\bm{)}+\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(v)\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime})$ .

#### Proof 3.16.

We show that whenever (a) does not hold, then (b) does. To this end, note that $\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(v)\,\bm{)}+\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(v)\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)}$ correponds to $\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)}$ with all the nodes from $\mathbf{P}$ taken out. Moreover, the pre-order of $\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(v)\,\bm{)}+\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(v)\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)}$ equals to the pre-order of $\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)}$ with the nodes of $\mathbf{P}$ taken out.

Next, let us compare the computations done by Shasha and Zhang’s recurrence scheme [SZ89] for the two similarities $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ and $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(v)\,\bm{)}+\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(v)\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime})$ . When computing $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ note that each time the recurrence scheme arrives to consider as next node of $\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)}$ some $u\in\mathbf{P}$ , we can ignore the case where $\mathsf{sub}(u)$ is aligned to the subtree of the current node in $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)}$ . As a consequence, we can assume that $u$ is always deleted. We conclude that we obtain the same computations as in the recurrence scheme for $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(v)\,\bm{)}+\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(v)\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime})$ .

#### Spines.

Let $\mathbf{F}$ be a forest. We define a spine as a path that starts at the root of one of the trees in $\mathbf{F}$ and ends in a leaf within that tree.

Now, consider a spine $\mathbf{S}\subseteq\mathbf{F}$ . For $s,q\in\mathbf{S}$ , we write $s\prec q$ if $s$ appears before $q$ in the root-to-leaf path, and we say $s$ precedes $q$ . Furthermore, we say that $s$ immediately precedes $q$ if there is no $r\in\mathbf{S}$ such that $s\prec r\prec q$ .

Lastly, suppose a spine $\mathbf{S}\subseteq\mathbf{F}$ is a path of the form $s_{1},\ldots,s_{m}$ . We observe that for all $i\in\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,m\,\bm{)}$ , a bi-order traversal enters $s_{i}$ before it enters $s_{i+1}$ , and leaves $s_{i+1}$ before it leaves $s_{i}$ . Consequently,

$$ \mathsf{l}(s_{1})<\mathsf{l}(s_{2})<\cdots<\mathsf{l}(s_{m})<\mathsf{r}(s_{m})<\cdots<\mathsf{r}(s_{2})<\mathsf{r}(s_{1}). $$

Moreover, $\mathsf{l}(s_{m})=\mathsf{r}(s_{m})-2$ , since $s_{m}$ is a leaf and the bi-order traversal leaves $s_{m}$ right after it enters it.

### 3.1 Min-Plus Products and Structured Instances

While Min-plus Matrix Multiplication (MUL) of $n\times n$ matrices is commonly conjectured to require $n^{3-o(1)}$ time, there have been several structured instances in which faster algorithms have been obtained, e.g. bounded entries [AGM97], (row/column) bounded-difference matrices [BGSV19], and (row/column) monotone matrices [VX20, GPVX21, CDXZ22] . Specifically, we focus on the class of monotone matrices.

#### Definition 3.17.

An $n\times n$ matrix is row-monotone if all entries are non-negative integers bounded by $\mathcal{O}(n)$ and each row of this matrix is non-decreasing. Similarly, we may define a column-monotone matrix.

When at least one of the matrices is row-monotone or column-monotone, there are sub-cubic algorithms for min-plus matrix multiplication [VX20, GPVX21, CDXZ22].

#### Theorem 3.18 ([CDXZ22]).

There is a (randomized) algorithm that computes the min-plus product $A*B$ in expected running time $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{(3+\omega)/2})$ , where $A$ is an $n\times n$ integer matrix and $B$ is a $n\times n$ row-monotone matrix. The result holds also when $B$ is a $n\times n$ column-monotone matrix. \lipicsEnd

The above result holds also when the rows or columns of the matrix are non-increasing.

We let $\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(n)$ denote the time required to multiply an $n\times n$ integer matrix with a $n\times n$ monotone matrix. Furthermore, let $\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(a,b,c,d)$ be the time required to multiply an $a\times b$ integer matrix with a $b\times c$ monotone matrix with all entries bounded by $d$ .

In our work, we will specifically work with rectangular matrices, and thus require the following simple lemma. We use $\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(a,b,c)$ to denote the time required to compute the $(\min,+)$ product between arbitrary $a\times b$ integer matrices and $b\times c$ integer matrices.

#### Lemma 3.19.

Suppose $n\geq m$ . Then,

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(n,m,m))=\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(m,n,m))=\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(m,m,n))=\mathcal{O}(n/m\cdot\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(m))\quad\text{and}\quad \displaystyle\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(n,m,m,m))=\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(m,n,m,m))=\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(m,m,n,m))=\mathcal{O}(n/m\cdot\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(m)). $$

We require the following bound on $(\min,+)$ -product between monotone matrices where the entries are bounded by $\mathrm{D}$ .

#### Lemma 3.20 ([Dür23]).

$\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(n,n,n,\mathrm{D})=\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{\mathrm{D}}n^{(2+\omega)/2})$ . \lipicsEnd

## 4 Reduction from Forest Edit Distance to APSP

In this section, we focus on proving Section 2.3 which we restate here and its unweighted version Theorem 4.1.

See 2.3

#### Theorem 4.1.

There is an $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(n)+n^{2+o(1)}g(n))$ time algorithm for unweighted FED where $n=\max(|\mathbf{F}|,|\mathbf{F}^{\prime}|)$ and $\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(n,n,n,\mathrm{D})=\mathcal{O}(f(n)g(\mathrm{D}))$ for some functions $f,g$ . \lipicsEnd

To approach FED, we adopt a conceptual shift, viewing it as a graph problem. Our perspective extends the computation of border-to-border distances in the alignment graph for string edit distance [LMS98, Tis06, ACS08, Kle05]. These distances precisely capture the edit distance between the prefix of one string and the suffix of the other, as well as between the entire string and all infixes of the second.

In this section, we denote by $\mathsf{dist}_{\mathbf{G}}(u,v)$ the longest distance (rather than shortest distance) from $u\in\mathbf{G}$ to $v\in\mathbf{G}$ in a directed weighted acyclic graph $\mathbf{G}$ . If $v$ is not reachable from $u$ , then $\mathsf{dist}_{\mathbf{G}}(u,v)=-\infty$ . This shift in definition is merely a notational change, given that we are working with a directed acyclic graph (by simply inverting the sign of the weights, one can switch between shortest and longest distances).

Throughout this section, we will give algorithms for the general setting of weighted tree edit distance, adding where appropriate optimizations that can be made for the unweighted tree edit distance problem. In Section 4.6, we describe how to compute FED efficiently on unbalanced instances, i.e. when one forest is significantly larger than the other. While Section 4.6 is necessary to obtain Section 1 for unweighted TED, readers interested only in Section 2.3 may skip it.

### 4.1 Generalizing alignment graphs

In this (sub)section, we extend the concept of the alignment graph for two strings to a broader framework capable of representing FED. Similar to the string case, the alignment graph we examine has a grid as its vertex set. This grid includes directed edges of zero weight, connnecting every grid point to its upper and right neighbour. Moreover, from each grid point $(i,j)$ , there is an additional edge connecting to a subgrid, whose lower-left corner is $(i+1,j+1)$ and whose top-right corner coincides with that of the entire grid.

#### Definition 4.2.

Given a forest $\mathbf{F}$ with pre-order $v_{1},\ldots,v_{|\mathbf{F}|}$ , we define $\pi_{\mathbf{F}}:\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,|\mathbf{F}|\,\bm{]}\rightarrow\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,|\mathbf{F}|+1\,\bm{]}$ as $\pi_{\mathbf{F}}(i)=\min\{j:j\geq i\text{ and }v_{j}\notin\mathsf{sub}(v_{i})\}$ . If no such $j$ exists, then $\pi_{\mathbf{F}}(i)=|\mathbf{F}|+1$ .

In other words, $\pi_{\mathbf{F}}(i)$ maps each node $v_{i}$ to the next node that pre-order visits after leaving the subtree $\mathsf{sub}(v_{i})$ (see Figure 6 for an example).

#### Definition 4.3 (See also [Tou05, BCH+07, MTWZU09]).

Given two forests $\mathbf{F}$ , $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ with pre-orders $v_{1},\ldots,v_{\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert}$ and $v_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,v_{\left\lvert\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\right\rvert}^{\prime}$ , and given a weight function $\mathrm{w}:D\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ such that $\mathbf{F}\times\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\subseteq D$ , we define the alignment graph $\bar{\mathbf{G}}=(\bar{V},\bar{E})$ w.r.t. $(\mathrm{w},\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime})$ as the directed weighted acyclic graph with

- • Vertex set $\bar{V}=\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,(\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert+1)\,\bm{]}\times\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,(\left\lvert\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\right\rvert+1)\,\bm{]}$ ;

- • Edge set $\bar{E}$ such that $\bar{e}=((u,u^{\prime}),(w,w^{\prime}))\in\bar{E}$ , if exactly one of the following holds: (a) $(w,w^{\prime})=(u,u^{\prime}+1)$ , (b) $(w,w^{\prime})=(u+1,u^{\prime})$ , or (c) $(w,w^{\prime})=(\pi_{\mathbf{F}}(u),\pi_{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}}(u^{\prime}))$ ;

- • Weight function $\bar{\mathrm{w}}$ such that $\bar{\mathrm{w}}(\bar{e})=0$ if $\bar{e}$ has the form (a) or (b), and $\bar{\mathrm{w}}(\bar{e})=\mathsf{sim}(\mathsf{sub}(v_{u}),\mathsf{sub}(v_{u^{\prime}}^{\prime}))$ if it has the form (c).

#### Definition 4.4.

Let $\bar{\mathbf{G}}$ be an alignment graph w.r.t $(\mathrm{w},\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime})$ where $\mathbf{F}$ , $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ are two forests with pre-orders $v_{1},\ldots,v_{\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert}$ and $v_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,v_{\left\lvert\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\right\rvert}^{\prime}$ . Given intervals $\bm{[}\,i\,\bm{.\,.}\,j\,\bm{]}\subseteq\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,(\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert+1)\,\bm{]},\bm{[}\,i^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,j^{\prime}\,\bm{]}\subseteq\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,(\left\lvert\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\right\rvert+1)\,\bm{]}$ , we denote with $\bar{\mathbf{G}}\bm{[}\,i\,\bm{.\,.}\,j\,\bm{]}\bm{[}\,i^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,j^{\prime}\,\bm{]}$ the alignment graph w.r.t. $(\mathrm{w},\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(v_{i})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(v_{j})\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(v_{i^{\prime}}^{\prime})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(v_{j^{\prime}}^{\prime})\,\bm{)})$ .

Note that $\bar{\mathbf{G}}\bm{[}\,i\,\bm{.\,.}\,j\,\bm{]}\bm{[}\,i^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,j^{\prime}\,\bm{]}$ does not necessarily correspond to the subgraph of $\bar{\mathbf{G}}$ induced by the vertex set $\bm{[}\,i\,\bm{.\,.}\,j\,\bm{]}\times\bm{[}\,i^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,j^{\prime}\,\bm{]}$ , as there might exist $z\in\bm{[}\,i\,\bm{.\,.}\,j\,\bm{)}$ such that $v_{z}\notin\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(v_{i})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(v_{j})\,\bm{)}$ . However, we can still derive the distances between any two nodes in the former graph from the distances in the latter graph, and vice versa.

To see this, observe that $\bar{\mathbf{G}}\bm{[}\,i\,\bm{.\,.}\,j\,\bm{]}\bm{[}\,i^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,j^{\prime}\,\bm{]}$ can be obtained from the subgraph of $\bar{\mathbf{G}}$ induced by the vertex set $\bm{[}\,i\,\bm{.\,.}\,j\,\bm{]}\times\bm{[}\,i^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,j^{\prime}\,\bm{]}$ by performing the following steps iteratively for each $z\in\bm{[}\,i\,\bm{.\,.}\,j\,\bm{)}$ where $v_{z}\notin\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(v_{i})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(v_{j})\,\bm{)}$ (and a similar process for each $z^{\prime}\in\bm{[}\,i^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,j^{\prime}\,\bm{)}$ where $v_{z^{\prime}}^{\prime}\notin\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(v_{i^{\prime}}^{\prime})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(v_{j^{\prime}}^{\prime})\,\bm{)}$ ): identify the vertex $(z,z^{\prime})$ with vertex $(z+1,z^{\prime})$ for all $z^{\prime}\in\bm{[}\,i^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,j^{\prime}\,\bm{]}$ . Throughout these iterations, $(i,j)$ denotes the vertex where the vertex $(i,j)$ of the subgraph of $\bar{\mathbf{G}}$ formed by the vertex set $\bm{[}\,i\,\bm{.\,.}\,j\,\bm{]}\times\bm{[}\,i^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,j^{\prime}\,\bm{]}$ might have potentially merged.

Let $\bar{\mathbf{G}}^{+z}$ be the graph before applying the step for some $z$ , and $\bar{\mathbf{G}}^{-z}$ denote the graph obtained after this step. Since $v_{z}\notin\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(v_{i})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(v_{j})\,\bm{)}$ , it follows that $\pi_{\mathbf{F}}(z)>j$ . Therefore, no vertex in $z\times\bm{[}\,i^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,j^{\prime}\,\bm{]}$ has an outgoing edge of the form (c) in $\bar{\mathbf{G}}^{+z}$ . Moreover, $\pi_{\mathbf{F}}^{-1}(z+1)=\varnothing$ , as otherwise it would contradict $\pi_{\mathbf{F}}(z)>j$ . Thus, no vertex in $(z+1)\times\bm{[}\,i^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,j^{\prime}\,\bm{]}$ has an incoming edge of the form (c) in $\bar{\mathbf{G}}^{+z}$ . It is not difficult to see that for any pair $(\bar{u},\bar{w})$ where at most one of $\bar{u},\bar{w}$ is contained in $\{z,z+1\}\times\bm{[}\,i^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,j^{\prime}\,\bm{]}$ , we have $\mathsf{dist}_{\bar{\mathbf{G}}^{+z}}(\bar{u},\bar{w})=\mathsf{dist}_{\bar{\mathbf{G}}^{-z}}(\bar{u},\bar{w})$ . Now, it is not difficult to see that if $\bar{u},\bar{w}\in\{z,z+1\}\times\bm{[}\,i^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,j^{\prime}\,\bm{]}$ , then the distance between $\bar{u}$ and $\bar{w}^{\prime}$ in $\bar{\mathbf{G}}^{+z}$ and $\bar{\mathbf{G}}^{-z}$ is zero if $\bar{w}$ is reachable from $\bar{w}$ in $\bar{\mathbf{G}}^{+z}$ and $\bar{\mathbf{G}}^{-z}$ , respectively, and $-\infty$ otherwise.

### 4.2 FED as border-to-border distances in an alignment graph

Our focus lies in computing paths from the lower-left to the upper-right border of an alignment graph.

Border-to-border Distances (BBD) Input: two forests $\mathbf{F}$ , $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ of size $\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert=n,\left\lvert\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\right\rvert=n^{\prime}$ , and a weight function $\mathrm{w}:D\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ such that $D\subseteq\mathbf{F}\times\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ . Output: $\mathsf{dist}_{\bar{\mathbf{G}}}(\bar{u},\bar{w})$ for all $\bar{u}\in\mathsf{B}^{\bot}(1,1,n+1,n^{\prime}+1)$ and $\bar{w}\in\mathsf{B}^{\top}(1,1,n+1,n^{\prime}+1)$ , where $\bar{\mathbf{G}}$ is the alignment graph w.r.t. $(\mathrm{w},\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime})$ .

We write $(\mathrm{w},\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime})$ -BBD for the BBD instance with input $\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ and $\mathrm{w}$ . Moreover, given a $(\mathrm{w},\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime})$ -BBD instance we say $\max(n,n^{\prime})$ is the size of the instance. Note, given a BBD instance of size $m$ , the output of such instance is of size $\mathcal{O}(m^{2})$ . Finally, we say that a $(\mathrm{w},\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime})$ -BBD instance has diameter $\mathrm{D}$ if $\mathsf{dist}_{\bar{\mathbf{G}}}(\bar{u},\bar{w})\leq\mathrm{D}$ for all $\bar{u}\in\mathsf{B}^{\bot}(1,1,n+1,n^{\prime}+1)$ and $\bar{w}\in\mathsf{B}^{\top}(1,1,n+1,n^{\prime}+1)$ i.e. if the alignment graph $\bar{\mathbf{G}}$ has diameter $\mathrm{D}$ .

#### Lemma 4.5.

Let $\mathbf{F}$ , $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ be forests with pre-orders $v_{1},\ldots,v_{\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert}$ and $v_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,v_{\left\lvert\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\right\rvert}^{\prime}$ . Then, FED on $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ can be reduced to BBD on $(\mathrm{w}_{\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}},\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime})$ , where $\mathrm{w}_{\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}}(i,i^{\prime})=\mathsf{sim}(\mathsf{sub}(v_{i}),\mathsf{sub}(v_{i^{\prime}}^{\prime}))$ for $(i,i^{\prime})\in\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert\,\bm{]}\times\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,\left\lvert\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\right\rvert\,\bm{]}$ .

#### Proof 4.6.

Recall Shasha and Zhang’s dynamic programming algorithm [SZ89] for computing the similarity between two forests $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ with pre-order $v_{1},\ldots,v_{|\mathbf{F}|}$ and $v_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,v_{|\mathbf{F}^{\prime}|}^{\prime}$ , described by the following recursive formula:

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F})=\left\{\begin{array}[]{@{\;}c@{\quad}l@{}}0,&\text{if $\mathbf{F}=\varnothing$ or $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}=\varnothing$,}\\
\max\left\{\begin{aligned} &\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\setminus v_{1},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}),\\
&\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\setminus v_{1}^{\prime}),\\
&\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\setminus\mathsf{sub}(v_{1}),\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\setminus\mathsf{sub}(v_{1}^{\prime}))+\mathsf{sim}(\mathsf{sub}(v_{1}),\mathsf{sub}(v_{1}^{\prime}))\end{aligned}\right\},&\text{otherwise}.\end{array}\right. $$

Consider arbitrary $\bm{[}\,i\,\bm{.\,.}\,j\,\bm{]}\subseteq\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,(\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert+1)\,\bm{]}$ and $\bm{[}\,i^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,j^{\prime}\,\bm{]}\subseteq\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,(\left\lvert\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\right\rvert+1)\,\bm{]}$ . Then, the dynamic programming computation of the longest path in $\bar{\mathbf{G}}\bm{[}\,i\,\bm{.\,.}\,j\,\bm{]}\bm{[}\,i^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,j^{\prime}\,\bm{]}$ between $(i,i^{\prime})$ and $(j,j^{\prime})$ aligns with the computation done by Shasha and Zhang’s scheme for $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(v_{i})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(v_{j})\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(v_{i^{\prime}}^{\prime})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(u_{j^{\prime}}^{\prime})\,\bm{)})$ . This allows us, given $x,y\in\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,(2\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert+1)\,\bm{]}$ such that $x\leq y$ , to find two nodes in the grid whose longest distance equals $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ . To this end, it suffices to define $i,j$ as the smallest $i$ such that $x\leq\mathsf{l}(v_{i})$ and the smallest $j$ such that $y\leq\mathsf{l}(v_{j})$ , obtaining $\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)}=\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(v_{i})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(v_{j})\,\bm{)}$ . Symmetrically, the same holds for $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ .

To conclude, note that whole-versus-infix similarities correspond to paths from the lower border to the upper border and from the left border to the right border, while prefix-versus-suffix similarities correspond to paths from the lower border to the right border and from the left border to the upper border.

To prove Section 2.3 and Theorem 4.1, we proceed to develop an algorithm for BBD instances. The weight function $\mathrm{w}$ in the algorithm we present can be an arbitrary function.

### 4.3 A decomposition scheme for forests

To solve such BBD instances, we employ a divide-and-conquer approach. Given a $(\mathrm{w},\mathbf{F},{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}})$ -BBD instance, we break it into several $(\mathrm{w},\mathbf{H},{\mathbf{H}^{\prime}})$ -BBD instances, for smaller forests $\mathbf{H}$ and $\mathbf{H}^{\prime}$ . We then merge these solutions to obtain the final solution for $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ . To derive these smaller instances, we utilize the decomposition scheme introduced by Mao [Mao22] in his subcubic algorithm for unweighted tree edit distance (though with a different parameter choice). This scheme, governed by a threshold parameter $\Delta$ , uses transitions of two types:

- I. transition from two synchronous forests $\mathbf{F}_{1}$ , $\mathbf{F}_{2}$ , both of size no less than $\Delta/3$ , to the synchronous subforest $\mathbf{F}=\mathbf{F}_{1}+\mathbf{F}_{2}$ ;

- II. transition from a synchronous forest $\mathbf{F}_{s}\subset\mathbf{F}$ such that $|\mathbf{F}\setminus\mathbf{F}_{s}|\leq\Delta$ to a synchronous forest $\mathbf{F}$ .

The subsequent two lemmas, the proofs of which we defer to Section 4.4, show how transitions in Mao’s decomposition scheme can be adapted to our scenario.

#### Lemma 4.7.

Suppose we are given a $(\mathrm{w},\mathbf{F},{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}})$ -BBD instance of size $m$ such that $\mathbf{F}=\mathbf{F}_{1}+\mathbf{F}_{2}$ .

Then, given the outputs of the $(\mathrm{w},{\mathbf{F}_{1}},{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}})$ -BBD instance and the $(\mathrm{w},{\mathbf{F}_{2}},{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}})$ -BBD instance, we can solve the $(\mathrm{w},\mathbf{F},{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}})$ -BBD instance in time $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(m))$ .

Furthermore, if the BBD instance has diameter $\mathrm{D}$ , we can solve the $(\mathrm{w},\mathbf{F},{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}})$ -BBD instance in time $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(m,m,m,\mathrm{D}))$ .

#### Lemma 4.8.

Suppose we are given a $(\mathrm{w},\mathbf{F},{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}})$ -BBD instance of size $m$ and a synchronous subforest $\mathbf{F}_{s}\subseteq\mathbf{F}$ of size $\left\lvert\mathbf{F}_{s}\right\rvert=n_{s}$ . Further, let $v_{1},\ldots,v_{\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert}$ be the pre-order of $\mathbf{F}$ , and let $i_{s}$ be such that $v_{i_{s}},\ldots,v_{i_{s}+n_{s}}$ is the pre-order of $\mathbf{F}_{s}$ . Define $\mathbf{F}_{\ell}=\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(v_{i_{s}})\,\bm{)}$ , $\mathbf{F}_{s}=\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(v_{i_{s}})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(v_{i_{s}+n_{s}+1})\,\bm{)}$ , and $\mathbf{F}_{r}=\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(v_{i_{s}+n_{s}+1})\,\bm{.\,.}\,2\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert+1\,\bm{)}$ .

Then, given the outputs of the four BBD instances $(\mathrm{w},\mathbf{F}_{\ell},{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}})$ -BBD, $(\mathrm{w},{\mathbf{F}_{s}},{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}})$ -BBD, $(\mathrm{w},{\mathbf{F}_{r}},{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}})$ -BBD, and $(\mathrm{w},{\mathbf{F}\setminus\mathbf{F}_{s}},{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}})$ -BBD, we can solve the $(\mathrm{w},\mathbf{F},{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}})$ -BBD instance in time $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(m))$ .

Furthermore, if the BBD instance has diameter $\mathrm{D}$ , we can solve the $(\mathrm{w},\mathbf{F},{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}})$ -BBD instance in time $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(m,m,m,\mathrm{D}))$ .

The decomposition scheme, together with Lemma 4.7 and Lemma 4.8, allows us to establish the following reduction from a $(\mathrm{w},\mathbf{F},{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}})$ -BBD instance of size $m$ to $\mathcal{O}(m^{2}/\Delta^{2})$ BBD instances, each of size at most $\Delta$ .

#### Lemma 4.9.

Suppose, we are given a $(\mathrm{w},\mathbf{F},{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}})$ -BBD instance of size $m$ , and a threshold $\Delta$ .

Then, in time $\mathcal{O}(m^{2})$ we can find forests $\mathbf{F}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{F}_{k}$ and $\mathbf{F}_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,\mathbf{F}_{k}^{\prime}$ , all of size at most $\Delta$ , such that $k=\mathcal{O}(m^{2}/\Delta^{2})$ and such that, given the output of the $(\mathrm{w},{\mathbf{F}_{i}},{\mathbf{F}_{i}^{\prime}})$ -BBD instance for all $i\in\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,k\,\bm{]}$ , we can solve the $(\mathrm{w},\mathbf{F},{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}})$ -BBD instance in time $\mathcal{O}(m^{2}/\Delta^{2}\cdot\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(m))$ .

Furthermore, if the BBD instance has diameter $\mathrm{D}$ , we can solve the $(\mathrm{w},\mathbf{F},{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}})$ -BBD instance in time $\mathcal{O}(m^{2}/\Delta^{2}\cdot\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(m,m,m,\mathrm{D}))$ .

To prove the simplified version of the lemma, we utilize Algorithm 1 (an adaptation of Algorithm 2 from [Mao22]) on the $(\mathrm{w},{\mathbf{F}},{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}})$ -BBD instance. Algorithm 1 applies recursively Mao’s transitions with the same parameter $\Delta$ on forests $\mathbf{H}\subseteq\mathbf{F}$ , until it is left with forests of size at most $\Delta$ . Algorithm 1 assumes that for $\mathbf{H}$ of size at most $\Delta$ the output of the $(\mathrm{w},{\mathbf{H}},{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}})$ -BBD instance can be retrieved directly (this assumption is equivalent to putting such instances among $\mathbf{F}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{F}_{d}$ ).

The correctness of Algorithm 1 follows directly from Lemma 4.7 and Lemma 4.8.

What remains to be demonstrated is a bound on $d$ and on the running time. For that purpose, notice that $d=\mathcal{O}(t_{\mathrm{I}}+t_{\mathrm{II}})$ and the running time is bounded by $\mathcal{O}((t_{\mathrm{I}}+t_{\mathrm{II}})\cdot\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(m))$ , where $t_{\mathrm{I}},t_{\mathrm{II}}$ is the number of times we apply transition of type I and II, respectively. If the diameter of $\bar{\mathbf{G}}$ is at most $\mathrm{D}$ , then we note that the running time is in fact bounded by $\mathcal{O}((t_{\mathrm{I}}+t_{\mathrm{II}})\cdot\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(m,m,m,\mathrm{D}))$ . To bound $t_{\mathrm{I}}+t_{\mathrm{II}}$ , we report here the argumentation from Section 4.2.2. of [Mao22].

For every transition of type I, we merge two forests each of size no less than $\Delta/3$ , yielding $t_{\text{I}}=\mathcal{O}(|\mathbf{F}|/\Delta)$ .

Now, for $t_{\text{II}}$ , let us decompose it into $t_{\text{II}}=t_{\text{II}}^{(1)}+t_{\text{II}}^{(2)}$ , where $t_{\text{II}}^{(1)}$ denotes the number of transitions of type II where $\mathbf{H}_{s}$ contains fewer than two trees or either $|\mathbf{L}_{\mathbf{H}_{s}}|$ or $|\mathbf{R}_{\mathbf{H}_{s}}|$ is less than $\Delta/3$ , and $t_{\text{II}}^{(2)}$ represents the number of transitions of type II where $\mathbf{H}_{s}$ contains at least two trees and both $|\mathbf{L}_{\mathbf{H}_{s}}|$ and $|\mathbf{R}_{\mathbf{H}_{s}}|$ are no less than $\Delta/3$ . For $t_{\text{II}}^{(1)}$ , we have $|\mathbf{H}\setminus\mathbf{H}_{s}|>\Delta/3$ , as otherwise, we would have not halted the removal process. Since $\mathbf{H}\setminus\mathbf{H}_{s}$ are disjoint across different type II transitions, we have $t_{\text{II}}^{(1)}=\mathcal{O}(|\mathbf{F}|/\Delta)$ . Regarding $t_{\text{II}}^{(2)}$ , observe that the subsequent transition will be of type I, so $t_{\text{II}}^{(2)}\leq t_{\text{I}}=\mathcal{O}(|\mathbf{F}|/\Delta)$ .

#### Corollary 4.11.

There is an algorithm that solves in time $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(m)+m^{2+o(1)})$ a $(\mathrm{w},{\mathbf{F}},{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}})$ -BBD instance of size $m$ .

Furthermore, if the BBD instance has diameter $\mathrm{D}$ , the algorithm runs in time $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(m,m,m,\mathrm{D})+m^{2+o(1)}g(D))$ , where $\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(m,m,m,\mathrm{D})=\mathcal{O}(f(m)g(\mathrm{D}))$ for some functions $f,g$ .

Thereby, we obtain an algorithm for the FED Problem where the running time is described by the recurrence

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{T}(m) \displaystyle\leq c_{1}\cdot(m/\Delta)^{2}\cdot\mathsf{T}(\Delta)+c_{2}\cdot(m/\Delta)^{2}\cdot\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(m)+c_{3}\cdot m^{2} \displaystyle=c_{1}\alpha^{2}\cdot\mathsf{T}(m/\alpha)+c_{2}\alpha^{2}\cdot\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(m)+c_{3}\cdot m^{2} $$

where $c_{1},c_{2},c_{3}$ , are the constants hidden in the number of problems we recurse on (parameter $k$ in Lemma 4.9), in the time needed to solve the $(\mathrm{w},{\mathbf{H}},{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}})$ -BBD instance, and the time needed to find the $k$ pairs of subforests, respectively. Now, for any $\varepsilon>0$ , we can choose a sufficiently large constant $\alpha$ such that

$$ \log_{\alpha}(c_{1}\alpha^{2})=\log_{\alpha}c_{1}+2<2+\varepsilon $$

and still $c_{2}\alpha^{2}=\mathcal{O}(1)$ . By applying the Master theorem, we conclude that $\mathsf{T}(m)=\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(m)+m^{2+o(1)})$ .

If the diameter is at most $\mathrm{D}$ , we instead have the recurrence,

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{T}(m) \displaystyle=c_{1}\alpha^{2}\cdot\mathsf{T}(m/\alpha)+c_{2}\alpha^{2}\cdot\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(m,m,m,\mathrm{D})+c_{3}\cdot m^{2} \displaystyle=c_{1}\alpha^{2}\cdot\mathsf{T}(m/\alpha)+O(f(m)g(\mathrm{D})). $$

By the master theorem, we can choose a sufficiently large constant $\alpha$ such that $\log_{\alpha}(c_{1}\alpha^{2})<2+\varepsilon$ for any $\varepsilon$ . By applying the Master theorem, we conclude that $\mathsf{T}(m)=\mathcal{O}((f(m)+m^{2+o(1)})g(D))=\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(m,m,m,\mathrm{D})+m^{2+o(1)}g(D))$ .

### 4.5 Computing spine mapping similarities

In this (sub)section we prove a lemma that will turn out to be useful in a special case appearing in Section 5. We prove it here, since in order to solve it we need to solve a BBD instance, similar to the $(\mathrm{w},{\mathbf{F}_{\setminus s}},{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}})$ -BBD instance appearing in Lemma 4.8.

#### Lemma 4.16.

Let $\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ be forests, let $\mathbf{S}\subseteq\mathbf{F}$ be a spine, and let $q\in\mathbf{S}$ .

Then, we can calculate the function $\mathsf{sim}_{q}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ for all $(x,x^{\prime})\in\mathsf{B}^{\bot}(1,1,\mathsf{l}(q),2\left\lvert\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\right\rvert+1)$ and $(y,y^{\prime})\in\mathsf{B}^{\top}(\mathsf{r}(q),1,2\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert+1,2\left\lvert\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\right\rvert+1)$ , where:

- • $\mathsf{sim}_{q}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})=\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ if there exists $t\in\mathbf{S}$ is such that $t\prec q$ and $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ aligns $\mathsf{sub}(t)$ to any subtree of $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ , and

### 4.6 Forest Edit Distance on Unbalanced Instances

In this section, we consider instances where one forest $\mathbf{F}$ is significantly larger than the other $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ . Without loss of generality, assume $n\geq n^{\prime}$ . We show that we can solve a restricted versions of the BBD problem more efficiently.

Left-Right Border-to-Border Distances (LRBBD) Input: two forests $\mathbf{F}$ , $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ of size $\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert=n,\left\lvert\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\right\rvert=n^{\prime}$ , and a weight function $\mathrm{w}:D\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ such that $D\subseteq\mathbf{F}\times\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ . Output: $\mathsf{dist}_{\bar{\mathbf{G}}}(\bar{u},\bar{w})$ for all $\bar{u}\in 1\times\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,n^{\prime}+1\,\bm{]}$ and $\bar{w}\in\mathsf{B}^{\top}(1,1,n+1,n^{\prime}+1)$ , where $\bar{\mathbf{G}}$ is the alignment graph w.r.t. $(\mathrm{w},\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime})$ .

We say $(n,n^{\prime})$ is the size of the LRBBD instance. We will solve the unbalanced LRBBD instance by decomposing the larger forest into forests of size at most $n^{\prime}$ using Mao’s decomposition algorithm (Algorithm 1), apply our BBD algorithm on each instance, and combining the results using the following two lemmas.

#### Lemma 4.18.

Suppose we are given a $(\mathrm{w},\mathbf{F},{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}})$ -LRBBD instance of size $(n,n^{\prime})$ such that $\mathbf{F}=\mathbf{F}_{1}+\mathbf{F}_{2}$ .

Then, given the outputs of the $(\mathrm{w},{\mathbf{F}_{1}},{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}})$ -LRBBD instance and the $(\mathrm{w},{\mathbf{F}_{2}},{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}})$ -LRBBD instance, we can solve the $(\mathrm{w},\mathbf{F},{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}})$ -LRBBD instance in time $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(n^{\prime},n^{\prime},n))$ .

Furthermore, if the LRBBD instance has diameter $\mathcal{O}(n^{\prime})$ , we can solve the $(\mathrm{w},\mathbf{F},{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}})$ -LRBBD instance in time $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(n^{\prime},n^{\prime},n,n^{\prime}))$ .

#### Lemma 4.19.

Suppose we are given a $(\mathrm{w},\mathbf{F},{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}})$ -LRBBD instance of size $(n,n^{\prime})$ and a synchronous subforest $\mathbf{F}_{s}\subseteq\mathbf{F}$ of size $\left\lvert\mathbf{F}_{s}\right\rvert=n_{s}$ . Further, let $v_{1},\ldots,v_{\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert}$ be the pre-order of $\mathbf{F}$ , and let $i_{s}$ be such that $v_{i_{s}},\ldots,v_{i_{s}+n_{s}}$ is the pre-order of $\mathbf{F}_{s}$ . Define $\mathbf{F}_{\ell}=\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(v_{i_{s}})\,\bm{)}$ , $\mathbf{F}_{s}=\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(v_{i_{s}})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(v_{i_{s}+n_{s}+1})\,\bm{)}$ , and $\mathbf{F}_{r}=\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(v_{i_{s}+n_{s}+1})\,\bm{.\,.}\,2\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert+1\,\bm{)}$ .

Then, given the outputs of the four LRBBD instances $(\mathrm{w},\mathbf{F}_{\ell},{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}})$ -LRBBD, $(\mathrm{w},{\mathbf{F}_{s}},{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}})$ -LRBBD, $(\mathrm{w},{\mathbf{F}_{r}},{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}})$ -LRBBD, and $(\mathrm{w},{\mathbf{F}\setminus\mathbf{F}_{s}},{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}})$ -LRBBD, we can solve the $(\mathrm{w},\mathbf{F},{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}})$ -LRBBD instance in time $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(n^{\prime},n^{\prime},n))$ .

Furthermore, if the LRBBD instance has diameter $\mathcal{O}(n^{\prime})$ , we can solve the $(\mathrm{w},\mathbf{F},{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}})$ -LRBBD instance in time $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(n^{\prime},n^{\prime},n,n^{\prime}))$ .

The decomposition scheme of Algorithm 1, together with Lemma 4.18 and Lemma 4.19, allows us to establish the following reduction from a $(\mathrm{w},\mathbf{F},{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}})$ -LRBBD instance of size $(n,n^{\prime})$ to $\mathcal{O}(n/\Delta)$ LRBBD instances, each of size at most $(\Delta,n^{\prime})$ for any threshold $\Delta$ .

#### Lemma 4.20.

Suppose, we are given a $(\mathrm{w},\mathbf{F},{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}})$ -LRBBD instance of size $(n,n^{\prime})$ and threshold $\Delta$ . Assume without loss of generality $n\geq n^{\prime}$ .

Then, there exist forests $\mathbf{F}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{F}_{k}$ all of size at most $\Delta$ , such that $k=\mathcal{O}(n/\Delta)$ and such that, given the output of the $(\mathrm{w},{\mathbf{F}_{i}},{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}})$ -LRBBD instance for all $i\in\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,k\,\bm{]}$ , we can solve the $(\mathrm{w},\mathbf{F},{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}})$ -LRBBD instance in time $\mathcal{O}(\frac{n^{2}}{\Delta n^{\prime}}\cdot\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(n^{\prime})$ .

Furthermore, if the LRBBD instance has diameter $\mathcal{O}(n^{\prime})$ , we can solve the $(\mathrm{w},\mathbf{F},{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}})$ -LRBBD instance in time $\mathcal{O}(\frac{n^{2}}{\Delta n^{\prime}}\cdot\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(n^{\prime}))$ .

#### Proof 4.21.

As in Lemma 4.9, we utilize Algorithm 1 on the $(\mathrm{w},{\mathbf{F}},{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}})$ -LRBBD instance. Algorithm 1 applies recursively Mao’s transitions with the same parameter $\Delta$ on forests $\mathbf{H}\subseteq\mathbf{F}$ , until it is left with forests of size at most $(\Delta,n^{\prime})$ . We use Lemma 4.18 and Lemma 4.19 to combine results as appropriate. The correctness of the algorithm follows directly from Lemma 4.18 and Lemma 4.19.

What remains to be demonstrated is a bound on $k$ and on the running time. For that purpose, notice that $k=\mathcal{O}(t_{\mathrm{I}}+t_{\mathrm{II}})$ where $t_{\mathrm{I}},t_{\mathrm{II}}$ is the number of times we apply transition of type I and II, respectively. As argued in Lemma 4.9, we have $k=\mathcal{O}(t_{\mathrm{I}}+t_{\mathrm{II}})=\mathcal{O}(n/\Delta)$ . Then, the running time can be bounded by

$$ \mathcal{O}\left(\frac{n}{\Delta}\cdot\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(n^{\prime},n^{\prime},n)\right)=\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{n^{2}}{\Delta n^{\prime}}\cdot\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(n^{\prime})\right). $$

If the diameter is at most $\mathcal{O}(n^{\prime})$ , we instead obtain

$$ \mathcal{O}\left(\frac{n}{\Delta}\cdot\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(n^{\prime},n^{\prime},n,n^{\prime})\right)=\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{n^{2}}{\Delta n^{\prime}}\cdot\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(n^{\prime})\right) $$

#### Corollary 4.22.

There is an algorithm that solves in time $(n/n^{\prime})^{1+o(1)}\cdot\left(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(n^{\prime})+n^{\prime 2+o(1)}\right)$ a $(\mathrm{w},{\mathbf{F}},{\mathbf{F}^{\prime}})$ -LRBBD instance of size $(n,n^{\prime})$ where $n\geq n^{\prime}$ .

Furthermore, if the LRBBD instance has diameter $\mathcal{O}(n^{\prime})$ , then the algorithm runs in time $(n/n^{\prime})^{1+o(1)}\cdot\left(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(n^{\prime})+n^{\prime 2+o(1)}g(n^{\prime})\right)$ where $\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(n^{\prime},n^{\prime},n^{\prime},\mathrm{D})=\mathcal{O}(f(n^{\prime})g(\mathrm{D}))$ .

#### Proof 4.23.

We apply Lemma 4.9 recursively with threshold $\Delta=n/\alpha$ for some constant $\alpha\geq 1$ on forest $\mathbf{F}$ . As before, for small enough instances when $n=O(n^{\prime})$ we can simply apply our algorithm for BBD and compute the output in $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(n^{\prime}))$ time. Thereby, we obtain an algorithm for the LRBBD Problem where the running time is described by the formula

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{T}(n,n^{\prime})=\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{n}{\Delta}\right)\mathsf{T}(\Delta,n^{\prime})+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{n^{2}}{\Delta n^{\prime}}\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(n^{\prime})\right). $$

Note that the recurrence terminates at $\mathsf{T}(n^{\prime},n^{\prime})=\mathcal{O}\left(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(n^{\prime})+n^{\prime 2+o(1)}\right)$ . By our choice of $\Delta$ , there exists a constant $C$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{T}(n,n^{\prime}) \displaystyle\leq\left(C\alpha\right)\mathsf{T}(n/\alpha,n^{\prime})+\left(C\alpha\frac{n}{n^{\prime}}\right)\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(n^{\prime}). $$

We choose a constant alpha such that $\log_{\alpha}(C\alpha)<1+\varepsilon$ for arbitrarily small $\varepsilon>0$ so that $\mathsf{T}(n,n^{\prime})=(n/n^{\prime})^{1+o(1)}\cdot\left(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(n^{\prime})+n^{\prime 2+o(1)}\right)$ .

When the diameter is at most $\mathcal{O}(n^{\prime})$ , we instead have the recurrence for some constant $C$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{T}(n,n^{\prime}) \displaystyle\leq\left(C\alpha\right)\mathsf{T}(n/\alpha,n^{\prime})+\left(C\alpha\frac{n}{n^{\prime}}\right)\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(n^{\prime}). $$

again with the recurrence terminating at $\mathsf{T}(n^{\prime},n^{\prime})=\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(n^{\prime})+n^{\prime 2+o(1)}g(n^{\prime}))$ . As before, we choose a constant $\alpha$ such that the time can be bounded by $\mathsf{T}(n,n^{\prime})=(n/n^{\prime})^{1+o(1)}\cdot\left(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(n^{\prime})+n^{\prime 2+o(1)}g(n^{\prime})\right)$ .

Finally, to conclude, we give an algorithm computing certain outputs of the FED problem efficiently, defined as the UFED problem.

There is an algorithm for UFED running in time $(n/n^{\prime})^{1+o(1)}\cdot\left(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(n^{\prime})+n^{\prime 2+o(1)}\right)$ where $\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert=n$ , $\left\lvert\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\right\rvert=n^{\prime}$ and $n\geq n^{\prime}$ .

## 5 Reduction from Spine Edit Distance to APSP

In this section, we focus on proving Section 2.3.

See 2.3

Similar to the previous one, we assume that there exists an algorithm computing the min/max-plus product of two $m\times m$ matrices in time $\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(m)$ . We use $\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(a,b,c)$ to the denote the time required to multiple an $a\times b$ matrix and a $b\times c$ matrix. As in Section 4, we describe our algorithm for general weighted tree edit distance instances, describing modifications for the unweighted case where necessary. To this end, recall that we use $\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(a,b,c,d)$ to denote the time required to multiply an $a\times b$ matrix with a $b\times c$ matrix where both matrices have entries bounded by $d$ and the latter matrix is row or column-monotone.

To formulate an algorithm for SED, we assume that $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ are trees. If they are not, we add virtual roots $t$ and $t^{\prime}$ , each labeled with a unique symbol, and include these in $\mathbf{S}$ and $\mathbf{S}^{\prime}$ respectively. This allows us to assume that the first nodes in $\mathbf{S}$ and $\mathbf{S}^{\prime}$ correspond to the first nodes in the pre-order traversals of $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ , respectively. For such new roots, we set $\mathsf{sim}(\mathsf{sub}(t),\mathsf{sub}(v^{\prime}))=-\infty$ for all $v^{\prime}\in\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\setminus\{t^{\prime}\}$ , even in the unweighted case, and similarly for $\mathsf{sim}(\mathsf{sub}(v),\mathsf{sub}(t^{\prime}))$ . This adjustment will not affect the algorithm we discuss, as these similarities only appear in the first column and row of some matrices we will work with. It is not difficult to see that we can compute the min/max-plus product of such matrices, in the same time as there would not be such column / row. Moreover, note that the solutions for SED on the original forests form a subset of the solutions on the new trees.

#### Definition 5.1.

Given two forests $\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ and four nodes $s,q\in\mathbf{S},s^{\prime},q^{\prime}\in\mathbf{S}^{\prime}$ such that $s\prec q$ and $s^{\prime}\prec q^{\prime}$ , set

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{B}^{\bot}_{\mathsf{l}}(s,s^{\prime},q,q^{\prime})\coloneqq\mathsf{B}^{\bot}(\mathsf{l}(s),\mathsf{l}(s^{\prime}),\mathsf{l}(q),\mathsf{l}(q^{\prime})), \displaystyle\mathsf{B}^{\top}_{\mathsf{l}}(s,s^{\prime},q,q^{\prime})\coloneqq\mathsf{B}^{\top}(\mathsf{l}(s),\mathsf{l}(s^{\prime}),\mathsf{l}(q),\mathsf{l}(q^{\prime})), \displaystyle\mathsf{B}^{\bot}_{\mathsf{r}}(s,s^{\prime},q,q^{\prime})\coloneqq\mathsf{B}^{\top}(\mathsf{r}(q),\mathsf{r}(q^{\prime}),\mathsf{r}(s),\mathsf{r}(s^{\prime})), \displaystyle\mathsf{B}^{\top}_{\mathsf{r}}(s,s^{\prime},q,q^{\prime})\coloneqq\mathsf{B}^{\bot}(\mathsf{r}(q),\mathsf{r}(q^{\prime}),\mathsf{r}(s),\mathsf{r}(s^{\prime})). $$

We can interpret these sets as follows. Consider the set $\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,(2\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert+1)\,\bm{]}\times\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,(2\left\lvert\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\right\rvert+1)\,\bm{]}$ . The sets $\mathsf{B}^{\bot}_{\mathsf{l}}(s,s^{\prime},q,q^{\prime})$ and $\mathsf{B}^{\top}_{\mathsf{l}}(s,s^{\prime},q,q^{\prime})$ are the lower left and upper right border of the subrectangle $\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(s)\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(q)\,\bm{]}\times\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(s^{\prime})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(q^{\prime})\,\bm{]}$ . On the other hand, $\mathsf{B}^{\bot}_{\mathsf{r}}(s,s^{\prime},q,q^{\prime})$ and $\mathsf{B}^{\top}_{\mathsf{r}}(s,s^{\prime},q,q^{\prime})$ are the upper right and lower left border of the subrectangle $\bm{[}\,\mathsf{r}(q)\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(s)\,\bm{]}\times\bm{[}\,\mathsf{r}(q^{\prime})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(s^{\prime})\,\bm{]}$ .

This allows us to define the following divide-et-impera scheme that we will use to solve SED.

Divide-et-Impera Spine Edit Distance (DISED) Input: $s\prec q\in\mathbf{S}$ , $s^{\prime}\prec q^{\prime}\in\mathbf{S}^{\prime}$ and (i) $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ for all $(x,x^{\prime})\in\mathsf{B}^{\top}_{\mathsf{l}}(s,s^{\prime},q,q^{\prime})$ and $(y,y^{\prime})\in\mathsf{B}^{\top}_{\mathsf{r}}(s,s^{\prime},q,q^{\prime})$ . (ii) $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathsf{sub}(q^{\prime}))$ for all $x,y\in\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(s)\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(q)\,\bm{]}$ . (iii) $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathsf{sub}(q^{\prime}))$ for all $x,y\in\bm{[}\,\mathsf{r}(q)\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(s)\,\bm{]}$ . (iv) $\mathsf{sim}(\mathsf{sub}(q),\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ for all $x^{\prime},y^{\prime}\in\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(s^{\prime})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(q^{\prime})\,\bm{]}$ . (v) $\mathsf{sim}(\mathsf{sub}(q),\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ for all $x^{\prime},y^{\prime}\in\bm{[}\,\mathsf{r}(q^{\prime})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(s^{\prime})\,\bm{]}$ . Output: The values (i) $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ for all $(x,x^{\prime})\in\mathsf{B}^{\bot}_{\mathsf{l}}(s,s^{\prime},q,q^{\prime})$ and $(y,y^{\prime})\in\mathsf{B}^{\bot}_{\mathsf{r}}(s,s^{\prime},q,q^{\prime})$ .

Such inputs and outputs consist of the values $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ for certain ranges of $x,y,x^{\prime},y^{\prime}$ . Every dotted horizontal line shows a combination of such ranges. The maximum number of nodes contained in any such set determines the size of the DISED instance.*

We write $(s,s^{\prime},q,q^{\prime})$ -DISED to denote an instance of the DISED Problem with input $s\prec q\in\mathbf{S}$ and $s^{\prime}\prec q^{\prime}\in\mathbf{S}^{\prime}$ .

Given an $(s,s^{\prime},q,q^{\prime})$ -DISED instance, we define its size as

$$ \max\Big\{\ \left\lvert\ \mathsf{sub}(s)\setminus\mathsf{sub}(q)\ \right\rvert\ ,\ \left\lvert\ \mathsf{sub}(s^{\prime})\setminus\mathsf{sub}(q^{\prime})\ \right\rvert\ \Big\}, $$

and global tree size as

$$ \min\Big\{\ \left\lvert\ \mathsf{sub}(s)\ \right\rvert\ ,\ \left\lvert\ \mathsf{sub}(s^{\prime})\ \right\rvert\ \Big\}. $$

We make two further remarks about an $(s,s^{\prime},q,q^{\prime})$ -DISED instance. First, input and output of an $(s,s^{\prime},q,q^{\prime})$ -DISED of size $m$ are of order $\mathcal{O}(m^{2})$ . Second, there exist two types of symmetry in the DISED Problem:

- (a) swapping the role of $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ does not change the input/output of the problem, we refer to this symmetry as swap symmetry; and

- (b) reversing $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ does not change the input/output of the problem, we refer to this symmetry as reverse symmetry.

These symmetries help simplify computations, reducing the need for different computations in symmetric cases.

### 5.1 Algorithm for DISED

In the following (sub)section, we present a divide-et-impera algorithm $\mathcal{A}_{\textsf{DISED}}$ solving DISED. The following two lemmas, the proof of which we defer to Section 5.3 and Section 5.4, motivate such an approach.

#### Lemma 5.2.

Consider an $(s,s^{\prime},q,q^{\prime})$ -DISED instance of size $m$ such that $s$ immediately precedes $q$ or $s^{\prime}$ immediately precedes $q^{\prime}$ . Then, we can solve the $(s,s^{\prime},q,q^{\prime})$ -DISED instance in time $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(m)+m^{2+o(1)})$ .

Furthermore, if the DISED instance is unweighted and has global tree size $\mathrm{D}$ , then the algorithm takes time $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(m,m,m,\mathrm{D})+m^{2+o(1)}g(\mathrm{D}))$ where $\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(m,m,m,\mathrm{D})=\mathcal{O}(f(m)g(\mathrm{D}))$ for some functions $f,g$ .

#### Lemma 5.3.

Suppose we are given an $(s,s^{\prime},q,q^{\prime})$ -DISED instance of size $m$ , and let $r\in\mathbf{S}$ be such that $s\prec r\prec q$ . Then, we can reduce the $(s,s^{\prime},q,q^{\prime})$ -DISED instance to the $(s,s^{\prime},r,q^{\prime})$ -DISED and $(r,s^{\prime},q,q^{\prime})$ -DISED instances in time $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(m)+m^{2+o(1)})$ .

Furthermore, if the DISED instance is unweighted and has global tree size $\mathrm{D}$ , then the reduction takes time $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(m,m,m,D)+m^{2+o(1)}g(\mathrm{D}))$ where $\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(m,m,m,\mathrm{D})=\mathcal{O}(f(m)g(\mathrm{D}))$ for some functions $f,g$ .

We can think of Lemma 5.2 and Lemma 5.3 as tools that allow us to cover the base case and to divide a larger problem into two smaller ones, respectively. Note, when we say ’reducing’, we are not merely referring to utilizing the output of the smaller instance to compute the larger instance. We are also accounting for the time and computation required to compute the input of the smaller instances. This input may not necessarily be an input of the larger instance but is essential for invoking any subroutine on the smaller instances. In these reductions, we assume that the output of a smaller instance is available to us as soon as we compute its inputs.

Intuitively, in Lemma 5.3 we would like to break down an instance $(s,s^{\prime},q,q^{\prime})$ -DISED into two instances $(s,s^{\prime},r,q^{\prime})$ -DISED and $(r,s^{\prime},q,q^{\prime})$ -DISED such that $\left\lvert\mathsf{sub}(s)\setminus\mathsf{sub}(r)\right\rvert\approx\left\lvert\mathsf{sub}(r)\setminus\mathsf{sub}(q)\right\rvert\approx\left\lvert\mathsf{sub}(s)\setminus\mathsf{sub}(q)\right\rvert/2$ . However, since this is not always possible, we need another division scheme that uses Lemma 5.3 as a subroutine.

#### Lemma 5.4.

Let be given an $(s,s^{\prime},q,q^{\prime})$ -DISED instance of size $m$ and a positive threshold $\Delta$ . Then, we can find $9m^{2}/\Delta^{2}$ DISED instances in time $\mathcal{O}(m^{2})$ , each of size at most $\Delta$ , such that given the input of all such instances, we can solve the $(s,s^{\prime},q,q^{\prime})$ -DISED instance in time $\mathcal{O}(m^{2}/\Delta^{2}\cdot(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(m)+m^{2+o(1)}))$ .

Furthermore, if the SED instance is unweighted and has global tree size $\mathrm{D}$ , the algorithm requires time $\mathcal{O}(m^{2}/\Delta^{2}\cdot(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(m,m,m,\mathrm{D})+m^{2+o(1)}g(\mathrm{D})))$ where $\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(m,m,m,\mathrm{D})=\mathcal{O}(f(m)g(\mathrm{D}))$ .

#### Proof 5.5.

We can simplify the proof to demonstrate the following: Given an $(s,s^{\prime},q,q^{\prime})$ -DISED instance of size $n$ and a threshold $\Delta$ , we can find in time $\mathcal{O}(m)$ a set $I\subseteq\mathbf{S}\times\mathbf{S}$ satisfying all of the following:

- • $|I|\leq 3m/\Delta$ ;

- • $s\preceq a\prec b\preceq q$ for $(a,b)\in I$ ;

- • $\left\lvert\mathsf{sub}(a)\setminus\mathsf{sub}(b)\right\rvert\leq\Delta$ for $(a,b)\in I$ ; and

- • the $(s,s^{\prime},q,q^{\prime})$ -DISED instance can be reduced to the $(a,s^{\prime},b,q^{\prime})$ -DISED instances for $(a,b)\in I$ in time $\mathcal{O}(m/\Delta\cdot(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(m)+m^{2+o(1)})+\mathcal{O}(m))$ . In the unweighted setting, we require time $\mathcal{O}(m/\Delta\cdot(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(m,m,m,\mathrm{D})+m^{2+o(1)}g(\mathrm{D}))+\mathcal{O}(m))$ .

Using swap symmetry, we can use the simplified version of the lemma first on the $(s,s^{\prime},q,q^{\prime})$ -DISED instance, and then apply it on the $(a,s^{\prime},b,q^{\prime})$ -DISED instances for all $(a,b)\in I$ , thereby proving the original statement of the lemma.

```
Input: two nodes $s,q\in\mathbf{S}$ such that $s\prec q$ , and a threshold $\Delta$ .
Output: a subset $s=r_{1}\prec r_{2}\prec\cdots\prec r_{d}=q\in\mathbf{S}$ .
1 $r_{1}\leftarrow s$ ;
2 $i\leftarrow 1$ ;
3 while $r_{i}\neq q$ do
4 Define $r_{i+1}\in\mathbf{S}$ to be the farthest node from $r_{i}$ on $\mathbf{S}$ such that $r_{i}\prec r_{i+1}\preceq q$ and $\left\lvert\mathsf{sub}(r_{i})\setminus\mathsf{sub}(r_{i+1})\right\rvert\leq\Delta$ . If no such $r_{i+1}$ exists, pick $r_{i+1}$ such that $r_{i}$ immediately precedes $r_{i+1}$ ;

6 return $\{r_{i}\}_{i}$ ;

```

To construct set $I$ , we employ Algorithm 2 on $s$ and $q$ with threshold $\Delta$ , yielding a sequence of spine nodes $s=r_{1}\prec r_{2}\prec\cdots\prec r_{d}=q$ . The algorithm guarantees that for each $i\in\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,d\,\bm{)}$ , either the $(r_{i},s^{\prime},r_{i+1},q^{\prime})$ -DISED instance has size at most $\Delta$ , or $r_{i}$ immediately precedes $r_{i+1}$ . To complete the reduction, we recursively solve $(r_{i},s^{\prime},r_{j},q^{\prime})$ -DISED instances for $i,j\in\bm{[}\,i\,\bm{.\,.}\,d\,\bm{]}$ with $i<j$ . This is achieved by selecting an arbitrary $i<k<j$ , and applying Lemma 5.3 to the $(r_{i},s^{\prime},r_{k},q^{\prime})$ -DISED and $(r_{k},s^{\prime},r_{j},q^{\prime})$ -DISED instances. Recursion stops when $j=i+1$ . At this point, if $r_{i}$ immediately precedes $r_{i+1}$ , we use Lemma 5.2; otherwise, we add $(r_{i},r_{i+1})$ to $I$ .

Therefore, starting with $i=1$ and $j=d$ , we achieve the desired reduction of the $(s,s^{\prime},q,q^{\prime})$ -DISED instance to $|I|\leq d-1$ DISED instances in time $\mathcal{O}((d-1)\cdot(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(m)+m^{2+o(1)}))$ . In the unweighted setting, the time is $\mathcal{O}((d-1)\cdot(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(m,m,m,\mathrm{D})+m^{2+o(1)}g(\mathrm{D}))$ .

To conclude the proof, it suffices to prove $d-1\leq 2m/\Delta+1\leq 3m/\Delta$ . To this end, we analyze Algorithm 2 in Algorithm 2. Here is an important observation: if $\left\lvert\mathsf{sub}(r_{i})\setminus\mathsf{sub}(r_{i+1})\right\rvert<\Delta$ , then either $d=i+1$ or $\left\lvert\mathsf{sub}(r_{i})\setminus\mathsf{sub}(r_{i+1})\right\rvert+\left\lvert\mathsf{sub}(r_{i+1})\setminus\mathsf{sub}(r_{i+2})\right\rvert>\Delta$ . Consequently, we iterate at most

$$ 2\left\lvert\mathsf{sub}(s)\setminus\mathsf{sub}(q)\right\rvert/\Delta+1\leq 2m/\Delta+1 $$

times in Algorithm 2, obtaining $d-1\leq 2m/\Delta+1$ .

#### Corollary 5.6.

There exists an algorithm $\mathcal{A}_{\textsf{DISED}}$ solving DISED running in time $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(m)+m^{2+o(1)})$ on instances of size $m$ .

Furthermore, if the DISED instance is unweighted and has global tree size $\mathrm{D}$ , then the algorithm requires time $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(m,m,m,\mathrm{D})+m^{2+o(1)}g(\mathrm{D}))$ where $\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(m,m,m,\mathrm{D})=\mathcal{O}(f(m)g(\mathrm{D}))$ .

#### Proof 5.7.

To devise such $\mathcal{A}_{\textsf{DISED}}$ , it suffices to apply recursively Lemma 5.4 with threshold $\Delta(m)=m/\alpha$ for a constant $\alpha\geq 1$ to be determined later. The base case is handled using Lemma 5.2. Thus, we obtain the following recurrence for the running time

where $c_{1}=9$ and we write out the constants $c_{2},c_{3}$ hidden in the time needed to solve the original $(s,s^{\prime},q,q^{\prime})$ -DISED instance, and to find the smaller DISED instances, respectively. and we bound the running time as in Corollary 4.11.

where the values coming from $\mathsf{sim}_{q}$ can be obtained in time $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(m)+m^{2+o(1)})$ ( $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(m,m,m,\mathrm{D})+m^{2+o(1)}g(\mathrm{D}))$ in the unweighted setting) using Lemma 4.16 on $\mathsf{sub}(r)$ , $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{r}(q^{\prime})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(s^{\prime})\,\bm{)}$ , $\mathbf{S}$ and $q$ . The proofs in the remaining part of this (sub)sections closely resemble the approach taken in Lemma 5.10. For brevity, we omit details beyond the initial case distinction in these proofs—specifically, how all distinct cases are put together into a single formula and how the distinct cases can be written as max-plus product between matrices (we still specify where the entries of these matrices can be retrieved from). #### Lemma 5.12.

Suppose we are provided with the input of an $(s,s^{\prime},q,q^{\prime})$ -DISED instance of size $m$ . Further, let $r\in\mathbf{S}$ such that $s\prec r\prec q$ . Then, we can compute $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ for all $(x,x^{\prime})\in(\mathsf{l}(r)\ \times\ \bm{[}\,\mathsf{r}(q^{\prime})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(s^{\prime})\,\bm{]})\ \cup\ (\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(s)\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(q)\,\bm{]}\ \times\ \mathsf{r}(q^{\prime}))$ and $(y,y^{\prime})\in(\mathsf{r}(r)\times\bm{[}\,\mathsf{r}(q^{\prime})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(s^{\prime})\,\bm{]})\ \cup\ (\bm{[}\,\mathsf{r}(q)\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(r)\,\bm{]}\ \times\ \mathsf{r}(s^{\prime}))$ in time $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(m)+m^{2+o(1)})$ .

Furthermore, if the DISED instance is unweighted and has global tree size $\mathrm{D}$ , then the algorithm requires time $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(m,m,m,\mathrm{D})+m^{2+o(1)}g(\mathrm{D}))$ where $\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(m,m,m,\mathrm{D})=\mathcal{O}(f(m)g(\mathrm{D}))$ .

#### Proof 5.13.

Refer to Figure 12 for a visualization of the ranges of $x,y,x^{\prime},y^{\prime}$ for which $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ needs to be computed. Observe in Figure 12 that the ranges of $x,y,x^{\prime},y^{\prime}$ for Lemma 5.12, are almost identical to the ones for Lemma 5.10. Thus, to prove Lemma 5.12, it suffices to compute the similarities for the ranges of $x$ that are left out in Lemma 5.10. That is, we need to compute $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,y\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ for

$$ (x,x^{\prime})\in(\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(s)\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(r)\,\bm{]}\times\mathsf{r}(q^{\prime}))\quad\text{and}\quad(y,y^{\prime})\in(\mathsf{r}(r)\times\bm{[}\,\mathsf{r}(q^{\prime})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(s^{\prime})\,\bm{]})\ \cup\ (\bm{[}\,\mathsf{r}(q)\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(r)\,\bm{]}\ \times\ \mathsf{r}(s^{\prime})). $$

To this end, observe that for such values of $x$ and $y$ , we have $\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)}=\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(r)\,\bm{)}+\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(r)\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)}$ . By Proposition 3.7, we have that $\mathsf{l}(r)\times\bm{[}\,\mathsf{r}(q^{\prime})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(s^{\prime})\,\bm{]}$ serves as an anchor set for $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ . Consequently, for such ranges of $x,y,x^{\prime},y^{\prime}$ we can write:

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})=\max_{z^{\prime}\in\bm{[}\,\mathsf{r}(q^{\prime})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(s^{\prime})\,\bm{]}:z^{\prime}\leq y^{\prime}}\Big\{\  \displaystyle\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(r)\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,z^{\prime}\,\bm{)}) \displaystyle+\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(r)\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,z^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})\ \Big\}. $$

Recall that we are considering the case $x^{\prime}=\mathsf{r}(q^{\prime})$ . Additionally, note that one of $y$ and $y^{\prime}$ is always fixed, specifically either $y=\mathsf{r}(r)$ or $y=\mathsf{r}(s^{\prime})$ . This means that, in the final expression, we are always working with at most two of $x,y,x^{\prime},y^{\prime}$ which are not fixed. As before, this expression can be computed as a max-plus product, with $z^{\prime}$ traversing the hidden dimension of the product. In this computation, the second summand is obtained from Lemma 5.10, while the first summand is calculated by applying Section 2.3 on $\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(s)\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(r)\,\bm{)}$ and $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{r}(q^{\prime})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(s^{\prime})\,\bm{)}$ . In the unweighted setting, we again observe that the matrices are monotone and have entries bounded by the global tree size $\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{D})$ , and apply Theorem 4.1 to compute FED.

### 5.5 Spine Edit Distance on Unbalanced Instances

In this section, we give an algorithm for Spine Edit Distance on unbalanced instances, where one tree, say $\mathbf{F}$ is significantly larger than $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ . In the following assume $\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert=n$ , $\left\lvert\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\right\rvert=n^{\prime}$ , and $n\geq n^{\prime}$ . For the smaller tree $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ , we let $r^{\prime}$ denote its root (i.e. top-most node of the spine) and $b^{\prime}$ denote the bottom-most node of the spine. In this setting, we compute a slightly restricted version of the divide et impera scheme for Spine Edit Distance.

Unbalanced Divide-et-Impera Spine Edit Distance (UDISED) Input: $s\prec q\in\mathbf{S}$ , $s^{\prime}\prec q^{\prime}\in\mathbf{S}^{\prime}$ and (i) $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ for all of the following indices: $\displaystyle\{\ (x,x^{\prime},y,y^{\prime}):(x,x^{\prime})\in\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(s)\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(r)\,\bm{]}\ \times\ \mathsf{l}(q^{\prime}),\ (y,y^{\prime})\in\mathsf{r}(r)\ \times\ \bm{[}\,\mathsf{r}(q^{\prime})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(s^{\prime})\,\bm{]}\ \}$ $\displaystyle\cup\quad$ $\displaystyle\{\ (x,x^{\prime},y,y^{\prime}):(x,x^{\prime})\in\mathsf{l}(r)\ \times\ \bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(s^{\prime})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(q^{\prime})\,\bm{]},\ (y,y^{\prime})\in\bm{[}\,\mathsf{r}(r)\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(s)\,\bm{]}\ \times\ \mathsf{r}(q^{\prime})\ \}$ $\displaystyle\cup\quad$ $\displaystyle\{\ (x,x^{\prime},y,y^{\prime}):(x,x^{\prime})\in\mathsf{l}(r)\ \times\ \bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(s^{\prime})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(q^{\prime})\,\bm{]},\ (y,y^{\prime})\in\mathsf{r}(r)\ \times\ \bm{[}\,\mathsf{r}(q^{\prime})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(s^{\prime})\,\bm{]}\ \}.$ (ii) $\mathsf{sim}(\mathsf{sub}(q),\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ for all $x^{\prime},y^{\prime}\in\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(s^{\prime})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(q^{\prime})\,\bm{]}$ . (iii) $\mathsf{sim}(\mathsf{sub}(q),\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ for all $x^{\prime},y^{\prime}\in\bm{[}\,\mathsf{r}(q^{\prime})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(s^{\prime})\,\bm{]}$ . Output: The values (i) $\mathsf{sim}(\mathsf{sub}(s),\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ for all $x^{\prime}\in\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(s^{\prime})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(q^{\prime})\,\bm{]},y^{\prime}\in\bm{[}\,\mathsf{r}(q^{\prime})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(s^{\prime})\,\bm{]}$ . (ii) $\mathsf{sim}(\mathsf{sub}(s),\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ for all $x^{\prime},y^{\prime}\in\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(s^{\prime})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(q^{\prime})\,\bm{]}$ . (iii) $\mathsf{sim}(\mathsf{sub}(s),\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,y^{\prime}\,\bm{)})$ for all $x^{\prime},y^{\prime}\in\bm{[}\,\mathsf{r}(q^{\prime})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(s^{\prime})\,\bm{]}$ .

On unbalanced instances, we will only decompose the larger graph $\mathbf{F}$ , so that we only handle $(s,s^{\prime},q,q^{\prime})$ -UDISED instances with $s^{\prime}=r^{\prime}$ and $q^{\prime}=b^{\prime}$ . Given such an instance, we define its size as $(m,n^{\prime})$ where

$$ m=\left\lvert\ \mathsf{sub}(s)\setminus\mathsf{sub}(q)\ \right\rvert. $$

In the following (sub)section, we present a divide-et-impera algorithm $\mathcal{A}_{\textsf{UDISED}}$ solving UDISED. The three lemmas, the proof of which we defer for now, that motivate such an approach are the following.

#### Lemma 5.18.

Consider an $(s,s^{\prime},q,q^{\prime})$ -UDISED instance of size $(m,n^{\prime})$ such that $m=\mathcal{O}(n^{\prime})$ . Then, we can solve the $(s,s^{\prime},q,q^{\prime})$ -UDISED instance in time $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(n^{\prime})+n^{\prime 2+o(1)})$ .

Furthermore, if the UDISED instance is unweighted, the algorithm requires time $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(n^{\prime})+n^{\prime 2+o(1)}g(n^{\prime}))$ where $\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(n^{\prime},n^{\prime},n^{\prime},\mathrm{D})=\mathcal{O}(f(n^{\prime})g(\mathrm{D}))$ .

#### Lemma 5.19.

Consider an $(s,s^{\prime},q,q^{\prime})$ -UDISED instance of size $(m,n^{\prime})$ such that $s$ immediately precedes $q$ . Then, we can solve the $(s,s^{\prime},q,q^{\prime})$ -UDISED instance in time $(m/n^{\prime})^{1+o(1)}\cdot(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(n^{\prime})+n^{\prime 2+o(1)})$ .

Furthermore, if the UDISED instance is unweighted, the algorithm requires time $(m/n^{\prime})^{1+o(1)}\cdot(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(n^{\prime})+n^{\prime 2+o(1)}g(n^{\prime}))$ where $\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(n^{\prime},n^{\prime},n^{\prime},\mathrm{D})=\mathcal{O}(f(n^{\prime})g(\mathrm{D}))$ .

#### Lemma 5.20.

Suppose we are given an $(s,s^{\prime},q,q^{\prime})$ -UDISED instance of size $m$ , and let $r\in\mathbf{S}$ be such that $s\prec r\prec q$ . Then, we can reduce the $(s,s^{\prime},q,q^{\prime})$ -UDISED instance to the $(s,s^{\prime},r,q^{\prime})$ -UDISED and $(r,s^{\prime},q,q^{\prime})$ -UDISED instances in time $(m/n^{\prime})^{1+o(1)}\cdot(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(n^{\prime})+n^{\prime 2+o(1)})$ .

Furthermore, if the UDISED instance is unweighted, the algorithm requires time $(m/n^{\prime})^{1+o(1)}\cdot(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(n^{\prime})+n^{\prime 2+o(1)}g(n^{\prime}))$ where $\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(n^{\prime},n^{\prime},n^{\prime},\mathrm{D})=\mathcal{O}(f(n^{\prime})g(\mathrm{D}))$ .

We now give an algorithm for the UDISED problem.

#### Lemma 5.21.

There exists an algorithm $\mathcal{A}_{\textsf{UDISED}}$ solving UDISED which runs in time $(m/n^{\prime})^{1+o(1)}\cdot\left(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(n^{\prime})+n^{\prime 2+o(1)}\right)$ on instances of size $(m,n^{\prime})$ .

Furthermore, if the UDISED instance is unweighted, then the algorithm only requires time $(m/n^{\prime})^{1+o(1)}\cdot\left(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(n^{\prime})+n^{\prime 2+o(1)}g(n^{\prime})\right)$ where $\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(n^{\prime},n^{\prime},n^{\prime},\mathrm{D})=\mathcal{O}(f(n^{\prime})g(\mathrm{D}))$ .

#### Proof 5.22.

It suffices to apply recursively (the simplified version of) Lemma 5.4 with threshold $\Delta(m)=m/\alpha$ for a constant $\alpha\geq 1$ to be determined later. In particular, we decompose only the larger tree $\mathbf{F}$ .

If $m=\mathcal{O}(n^{\prime})$ , we simply apply Lemma 5.18 to the instance. Otherwise, we proceed to construct a set $I\subseteq\mathbf{S}\times\mathbf{S}$ using Algorithm 2 with threshold $\Delta$ yielding a sequence of spine nodes $s=r_{1}\prec r_{2}\prec\cdots\prec r_{d}=q$ . The algorithm guarantees for each $i\in\bm{[}\,1\,\bm{.\,.}\,d\,\bm{)}$ , either $(r_{i},s^{\prime},r_{i+1},q^{\prime})$ -UDISED has size at most $(\Delta,n^{\prime})$ or $r_{i}$ immediately precedes $r_{i+1}$ . To complete the reduction we recursively solve $(r_{i},s^{\prime},r_{i+1},q^{\prime})$ -UDISED instances, which requires total time $\mathcal{O}(d\mathsf{T}(\Delta,n^{\prime}))$ in the former case and $(m/n^{\prime})^{1+o(1)}\cdot\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(n^{\prime})$ in the latter case, since the combined size of the instances in the latter case is at most $(m,n^{\prime})$ . Note that there are at most $d$ instances to recombine, and thus recombining the instances require $\mathcal{O}(d(m/n^{\prime})^{1+o(1)}\cdot\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(n^{\prime}))$ .

Thus, we obtain the following recurrence by using $d\leq 3m/\Delta$ so that for some constant $C$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{T}(m) \displaystyle=\mathcal{O}(3m/\Delta\mathsf{T}(\Delta,n^{\prime})+(m/n^{\prime})^{1+o(1)}\cdot(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(n^{\prime})+n^{\prime 2+o(1)})) \displaystyle\leq 3C\alpha\mathsf{T}(m/\alpha,n^{\prime})+(m/n^{\prime})^{1+o(1)}\cdot(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(n^{\prime})+n^{\prime 2+o(1)}). $$

For any $\varepsilon>0$ , we can choose a sufficiently large constant $\alpha$ such that $\log_{\alpha}(3C\alpha)<1+\varepsilon$ .
