As in Section 2.3, we fix $s,s^{\prime}$ as the roots of $\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ and $q,q^{\prime}$ as the last nodes in the spines of $\mathbf{S},\mathbf{S}^{\prime}$ . The algorithm then runs $\mathcal{A}_{\textsf{UDISED}}$ on the $(s,s^{\prime},q,q^{\prime})$ -UDISED instance and thus takes time $(n/n^{\prime})^{1+o(1)}\cdot\left(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(n^{\prime})+n^{\prime 2+o(1)}\right)$ . In the unweighted setting, UDISED only takes time $(n/n^{\prime})^{1+o(1)}\cdot\left(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(n^{\prime})+n^{\prime 2+o(1)}g(n^{\prime})\right)$ .

We claim that this computes all required outputs $\mathsf{sim}(\mathsf{sub}(v),\mathsf{sub}(v^{\prime}))$ for $(v,v^{\prime})\in\mathbf{S}\times\mathbf{S}^{\prime}$ . Fix a pair $(v,v^{\prime})\in\mathbf{S}\times\mathbf{S}^{\prime}$ . Assume we always recurse on the instance satisfying $u\preceq v\prec w$ and $u^{\prime}\preceq v^{\prime}\prec w^{\prime}$ until we reach one of the following:

- • A $(u,u^{\prime},w,w^{\prime})$ -UDISED where $u$ immediately precedes $w$ and $u^{\prime}\preceq v^{\prime}\prec w^{\prime}$ . In this case $\mathsf{sim}(\mathsf{sub}(v),\mathsf{sub}(v^{\prime}))$ is among the outputs of the UDISED instance.

- • A $(u,u^{\prime},w,w^{\prime})$ -DISED. In this case, the outputs are computed following identical arguments as Section 2.3.

To conclude the proof, we bound the run-time of obtaining the inputs to the $(s,s^{\prime},q,q^{\prime})$ -UDISED instance. We begin with Input (i) and rewrite the input indices as

$$ \displaystyle\{\ (x,x^{\prime},y,y^{\prime}):(x,x^{\prime})\in\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(s)\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(q)\,\bm{]}\times\mathsf{l}(q^{\prime}),(y,y^{\prime})\in\mathsf{r}(q)\times\bm{[}\,\mathsf{r}(q^{\prime})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(s^{\prime})\,\bm{]}\ \} \displaystyle\cup\quad \displaystyle\{\ (x,x^{\prime},y,y^{\prime}):(x,x^{\prime})\in\mathsf{l}(q)\times\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(s^{\prime})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(q^{\prime})\,\bm{]},\ (y,y^{\prime})\in\bm{[}\,\mathsf{r}(q)\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(s)\,\bm{]}\times\mathsf{r}(q^{\prime})\ \} \displaystyle\cup\quad \displaystyle\{\ (x,x^{\prime},y,y^{\prime}):(x,x^{\prime})\in\mathsf{l}(q)\times\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(s^{\prime})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(q^{\prime})\,\bm{]},\ (y,y^{\prime})\in\mathsf{r}(q)\times\bm{[}\,\mathsf{r}(q^{\prime})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(s^{\prime})\,\bm{]}\ \}. $$

We can compute the similarity for the various subsets of indices (26), (27) and (28) as follows.

- • For (26), we apply Theorem 4.24 to the forests $\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(s)\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(q)\,\bm{)}$ and $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(q^{\prime})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(s^{\prime})\,\bm{)}$ . Note that both forests do not contain any spine nodes so we are given as inputs to the SED instance all required inputs to the UFED instance, and thus we may compute $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,x\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(q)\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(q^{\prime})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(s^{\prime})\,\bm{)})$ in time $(n/n^{\prime})^{1+o(1)}\cdot\left(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(n^{\prime})+n^{\prime 2+o(1)}\right)$ .

- • For (27), we likewise apply Theorem 4.24 but this time to the forests $\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(q)\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(s)\,\bm{)}$ and $\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(s^{\prime})\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(q^{\prime})\,\bm{)}$ . Following similar arguments as (26), we note that the required similarities $\mathsf{sim}(\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{l}(q)\,\bm{.\,.}\,y\,\bm{)},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\bm{[}\,x^{\prime}\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(q^{\prime})\,\bm{)})$ are given by Output (2) in time $(n/n^{\prime})^{1+o(1)}\cdot\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MUL}}(n^{\prime})$ .

- • For (28), we observe that $\mathsf{sub}(q)=q$ is a single node so we can compute the necessary entries using dynamic programming in $O(n^{\prime 2})$ time.

Finally, for Inputs (ii), (iii) we again note that $\mathsf{sub}(q)=q$ is a single node so we can obtain the necessary entries in $O(n^{\prime 2})$ time.

In the unweighted setting, computing UFED takes time $(n/n^{\prime})^{1+o(1)}\cdot\left(\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{MonMUL}}(n^{\prime})+n^{\prime 2+o(1)}g(n^{\prime})\right)$ .

## 6 Reduction from Spine Edit Distance to Tree Edit Distance

In this section, we prove Lemma 2.1, i.e., we reduce TED on SED.77 7 Although [BGHS19] briefly mentions the existence of this reduction, it does so only in a footnote.

See 2.1

We will first reduce the following variant of SED to SED:

Spine to All-Subtree Tree Edit Distance (SASED) Input: Two forests $\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ , a spine $\mathbf{S}\subseteq\mathbf{F}$ , and $\mathsf{sim}(\mathsf{sub}(v),\mathsf{sub}(v^{\prime}))$ for all $(v,v^{\prime})\in(\mathbf{F}\setminus\mathbf{S})\times\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ Output: $\mathsf{sim}(\mathsf{sub}(v),\mathsf{sub}(v^{\prime}))$ for all $(v,v^{\prime})\in\mathbf{F}\times\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ .

Utilizing the above reduction, we further reduce All-Subtrees-TED to SED, which we define as a more general problem than TED.

All Subtrees Tree Edit Distance ( $\textsf{All-Subtrees-TED})$ Input: Two forests $\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ . Output: $\mathsf{sim}(\mathsf{sub}(v),\mathsf{sub}(v^{\prime}))$ for all $(v,v^{\prime})\in\mathbf{F}\times\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ .

Our reduction is based on a tree decomposition similar to the well-known heavy path decomposition introduced by Harel and Tarjan [HT84]. For our purposes, we can formulate this decomposition as follows.

#### Proposition 6.1.

Let $\mathbf{F}$ be a forest. Then, there exists a spine $\mathbf{S}\subseteq\mathbf{F}$ ending at leaf $v$ satisfying

$$ \left\lvert\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,0\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(v)\,\bm{)}\right\rvert\leq\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert/2\quad\text{and}\quad\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{r}(v)\,\bm{.\,.}\,2\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert+1\,\bm{)}\right\rvert\leq\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert/2. $$

Here, $\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,0\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(v)\,\bm{)}$ and $\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{r}(v)\,\bm{.\,.}\,2\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert+1\,\bm{)}$ are exactly the nodes right and left w.r.t. $\mathbf{S}$ , respectively.

#### Proof 6.2.

Attach to $\mathbf{F}$ a new root such that $\mathbf{F}$ becomes a tree. We start by walking from the (new) root of $\mathbf{F}$ to a leaf. At each node $u$ , we continue the walk to the rightmost child $w$ of $u$ that satisfies $\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,0\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(w)\,\bm{)}\right\rvert\leq\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert/2$ .

We aim to maintain the invariant $\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,0\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(u)\,\bm{)}\right\rvert\leq\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert/2$ and $\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{r}(u)\,\bm{.\,.}\,2\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert+1\,\bm{)}\right\rvert\leq\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert/2$ . This invariant clearly holds at the beginning, and ultimately, the walk traces out a spine $\mathbf{S}$ with the properties stated.

For the inductive step, observe that, by the definition of this walk, moving from $u$ to the next node $w$ ensures $\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,0\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(w)\,\bm{)}\right\rvert\leq\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert/2$ . We must show that $\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{r}(w)\,\bm{.\,.}\,2\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert+1\,\bm{)}\right\rvert\leq\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert/2$ . To do this, we consider two cases. If $w$ has a right sibling $w^{\prime}$ , then $\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,0\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(w)\,\bm{)}\right\rvert=\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,0\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(w^{\prime})\,\bm{)}\right\rvert\geq\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert/2$ , which leads to $\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{r}(w)\,\bm{.\,.}\,2\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert+1\,\bm{)}\right\rvert=\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert-\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,0\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{r}(w)\,\bm{)}\right\rvert\leq\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert/2$ . On the other hand, if $w$ is the rightmost child of $u$ , then $\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{r}(w)\,\bm{.\,.}\,2\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert+1\,\bm{)}\right\rvert=\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{r}(u)\,\bm{.\,.}\,2\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert+1\,\bm{)}\right\rvert\leq\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert/2$ .

#### Definition 6.3.

For each forest $\mathbf{F}$ , fix an arbitrary spine $\mathbf{S}$ ending in a leaf $v$ satisfying Proposition 6.1. Define $\mathbf{L}(\mathbf{F})\coloneqq\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,0\,\bm{.\,.}\,\mathsf{l}(v)\,\bm{)}$ and $\mathbf{R}(\mathbf{F})\coloneqq\mathbf{F}\bm{[}\,\mathsf{r}(v)\,\bm{.\,.}\,2\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert+1\,\bm{)}$ , for the subforest containing the nodes on the left and right w.r.t. the fixed spine $\mathbf{S}$ , respectively. If $\mathbf{F}=\varnothing$ is empty, then, we set $\mathbf{L}(\mathbf{F})=\mathbf{R}(\mathbf{F})=\varnothing$ .

We are now ready to show the reduction from SASED to SED.

#### Lemma 6.4.

Suppose there exists an algorithm for SED on two forests $\mathbf{H},\mathbf{H}^{\prime}$ running in time $\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{SED}}(m,m^{\prime})=\mathcal{O}(f(m)g(m^{\prime}))$ , where $m=|\mathbf{H}|,m^{\prime}=|\mathbf{H}^{\prime}|$ and $f(m)=\Omega(m),g(m^{\prime})=\Omega(m^{\prime})$ are some functions. Then, there is an algorithm for SASED on two forests $\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ running in time $\mathcal{O}(f(n)g(n^{\prime})\log n^{\prime})$ , where $n=|\mathbf{F}|,n^{\prime}=|\mathbf{F}^{\prime}|$ .

#### Proof 6.5.

In the base case, if $n^{\prime}=0$ , we can trivially return an empty set.

In general, we find a spine $\mathbf{S}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ using Proposition 6.1, and obtain $\mathbf{L}(\mathbf{F}^{\prime})$ and $\mathbf{R}(\mathbf{F}^{\prime})$ according to Definition 6.3. Then we recursively solve SASED on $(\mathbf{F},\mathbf{L}(\mathbf{F}^{\prime}))$ and $(\mathbf{F},\mathbf{R}(\mathbf{F}^{\prime}))$ .

Note that with the input of the SASED instance $(\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime})$ , and the outputs of the SASED instances $(\mathbf{F},\mathbf{L}(\mathbf{F}^{\prime}))$ and $(\mathbf{F},\mathbf{R}(\mathbf{F}^{\prime}))$ , we have collected all inputs for SED between $(\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime})$ , so we can run the SED algorithm to finish the algorithm in $\mathcal{O}(f(n)g(n^{\prime}))$ time.

The running time $\mathsf{T}(n,n^{\prime})$ of the algorithm can be formulated as the following formula:

$$ \mathsf{T}(n,n^{\prime})=2\mathsf{T}(n,n^{\prime}/2)+\mathcal{O}(f(n)g(n^{\prime})), $$

which can be upper bounded by $\mathsf{T}(n,n^{\prime})=\mathcal{O}(f(n)g(n^{\prime})\log n^{\prime})$ .

Now we proceed to show the reduction from All-Subtrees-TED to SED.

#### Lemma 6.6.

Suppose there exists an algorithm for SED on two forests $\mathbf{H},\mathbf{H}^{\prime}$ running in time $\mathsf{T}_{\textsf{SED}}(m,m^{\prime})=\mathcal{O}(f(m)g(m^{\prime}))$ , where $m=|\mathbf{H}|,m^{\prime}=|\mathbf{H}^{\prime}|$ and $f(m)=\Omega(m),g(m^{\prime})=\Omega(m^{\prime})$ are some functions. Then, there is an algorithm for All-Subtrees-TED on two forests $\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ running in time $\mathcal{O}(f(n)g(n^{\prime})\log^{2}\max(n^{\prime},n))$ , where $n=\left\lvert\mathbf{F}\right\rvert,n^{\prime}=\left\lvert\mathbf{F}^{\prime}\right\rvert$ .

#### Proof 6.7.

In the base case, if $n=0$ or $n^{\prime}=0$ , we can simply return an empty set.

In general, given $\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime}$ , we use Proposition 6.1 and Definition 6.3 to prepare $\mathbf{S},\mathbf{L}(\mathbf{F}),\mathbf{R}(\mathbf{F}),\mathbf{S}^{\prime},\mathbf{L}(\mathbf{F}^{\prime}),\mathbf{R}(\mathbf{F}^{\prime})$ . We recursively solve All-Subtrees-TED in $4$ instances $(\mathbf{L}(\mathbf{F}),\mathbf{L}(\mathbf{F}^{\prime})),(\mathbf{L}(\mathbf{F}),\mathbf{R}(\mathbf{F}^{\prime})),(\mathbf{R}(\mathbf{F}),\mathbf{L}(\mathbf{F}^{\prime})),(\mathbf{R}(\mathbf{F}),\mathbf{R}(\mathbf{F}^{\prime}))$ .

Next, we apply Lemma 6.4 on inputs $(\mathbf{F},\mathbf{L}(\mathbf{F}^{\prime})),(\mathbf{F},\mathbf{R}(\mathbf{F}^{\prime})),(\mathbf{F}^{\prime},\mathbf{L}(\mathbf{F})),(\mathbf{F}^{\prime},\mathbf{R}(\mathbf{F}))$ . Note that applying Lemma 6.4 on the first two instances clearly takes time $\mathcal{O}(f(n)g(n^{\prime})\log n^{\prime})$ . Applying Lemma 6.4 directly on the last two instances would take time $\mathcal{O}(f(n^{\prime})g(n)\log n)$ . However, notice that by symmetry, if there exists a SED algorithm with running time $\mathcal{O}(f(m)g(m^{\prime}))$ , there is also a SED algorithm with running time $\mathcal{O}(g(m)f(m^{\prime}))$ by swapping the two input forests. Applying Lemma 6.4 on the last two instances assuming the existence of a SED algorithm with running time $\mathcal{O}(g(m)f(m^{\prime}))$ gives us a running time $\mathcal{O}(f(n)g(n^{\prime})\log n)$ . Hence, the overall running time of applying Lemma 6.4 is $\mathcal{O}(f(n)g(n^{\prime})\log\max(n^{\prime},n))$ .

Finally, at this point we have collected all required inputs for SED on input $(\mathbf{F},\mathbf{F}^{\prime})$ , so we can apply the assume SED algorithm in time $\mathcal{O}(f(n)g(n^{\prime}))$ .

Let $\mathsf{T}(n,n^{\prime})$ be the running time of this algorithm, then it can be written as

$$ \mathsf{T}(n,n^{\prime})=4\mathsf{T}(n/2,n^{\prime}/2)+\mathcal{O}(f(n)g(n^{\prime})\log\max(n^{\prime},n)), $$

which can be upper bounded by $\mathsf{T}(n,n^{\prime})=\mathcal{O}(f(n)g(n^{\prime})\log^{2}\max(n^{\prime},n))$ .

Indeed, Lemma 2.1 follows directly from Lemma 6.6.
